templates.title: Lost trips after a match: who cancelled, and how long the rider had waited
templates.subtopic: one row per entity before grouping, last event per key, bucketing

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace matches each trip request to a driver. Sometimes the match falls apart after it was made: the driver cancels and dispatch looks for another driver (a re-match), the rider gives up, or dispatch gives up. The marketplace-health team wants to know, for trips lost after a match, who ended them and how long the rider had been waiting since they were first told a car was coming, without counting a request twice because it was re-matched.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns city, cancelled_by, wait_bucket, lost_requests, rematched_requests, max_wait_s for every (city, cancelled_by, wait_bucket) with at least one lost trip, ordered by city, cancelled_by, then bucket from the shortest wait to the longest. A request's events are its dispatch_events in (event_ts, event_id) order. A request is a lost trip when it has at least one MATCHED event, no PICKED_UP event, and at least one CANCELLED event. It counts once, under the party of its last CANCELLED event (cancelled_by). Its wait is the number of seconds from its first MATCHED event to that last cancellation. wait_bucket is '{{bucket_a}}' for a wait under {{b1_s}} seconds, '{{bucket_b}}' from {{b1_s}} up to but not including {{b2_s}} seconds, and '{{bucket_c}}' from {{b2_s}} seconds on. lost_requests counts lost trips; rematched_requests counts those that were matched to at least two distinct drivers; max_wait_s is the longest wait in the group. {{party_rule}} {{ingest_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A request counts once however many times it was matched or cancelled. A request cancelled before any match, and a request that was re-matched after a driver cancelled and then picked up, are not lost trips after a match. The sample has {{n_requests}} requests and {{n_events}} events; a large marketplace has many millions a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical cities, identifiers, timings and bucket edges. Real dispatch has more states (driver arrived, rider no-show, cancellation fees); this exercise uses only the events shown. All timestamps are UTC instants.
sections.criteria: One row per request before grouping; lost trip defined by a match, no pickup and a cancellation; the last cancellation by (event_ts, event_id) decides the party; the wait from the first match, not the latest; buckets that include their lower edge; re-matches by distinct drivers (duplicated rows at Very Hard); deterministic ordering by bucket rank rather than label text; can discuss rates, grace periods and late data.

clarifications.q: A driver cancels, a second driver is matched, then the rider cancels. Whose is it?
clarifications.a: The rider's: the last cancellation ended the request. It is also a re-matched request.

clarifications.q: Does a re-match reset the wait?
clarifications.a: No. The wait runs from the first MATCHED event: the rider has been waiting since then.

clarifications.q: Is a wait of exactly {{b1_s}} seconds in '{{bucket_a}}'?
clarifications.a: No. A bucket includes its lower edge, so it is in '{{bucket_b}}'.

clarifications.q: A driver cancelled, the request was re-matched and the rider was picked up.
clarifications.a: Not a lost trip, so it is not in the report.

clarifications.q: Two cancellations of one request have the same event_ts.
clarifications.a: Order by (event_ts, event_id): the higher event_id is the later one.

hints: Reduce to one row per request first: its first match time, the number of distinct drivers matched, and whether it was picked up.
DISTINCT ON (request_id) … ORDER BY request_id, event_ts DESC, event_id DESC picks each request's last cancellation.
Compute a bucket number with CASE, group and order by it, and derive the label from it.
followups: Product asks for cancellation rates, not counts. What is the denominator for a driver-cancellation rate, and why is it different from the one for riders?
A rider who cancels within a short grace period after a match pays no fee in many marketplaces. How would you report cancellations inside and outside a grace period without counting any twice?
Events from phones can arrive a day late. How would you build this as a daily table that is correct after late data, and when would you call a day final?
At hundreds of millions of events a day across many cities, how would you partition dispatch_events, and what goes wrong when one request's events land in two daily partitions?

rules.ask: A request was matched three times and cancelled three times. How many times does it appear in your counts?
The first driver cancelled after four minutes and a second driver was matched. When did the rider's wait start?
A phone uploads its events an hour late. Which cancellation does ordering by event_id pick as the last one?
This report measures the wait from the first match. What would measuring from the request add, and which team would want that instead?
A client retry wrote the same match twice. Is that request re-matched in your query?

templates.title: Driver utilisation by hour from status changes
templates.subtopic: LEAD to turn changes into spans, clipping to a window, splitting at hour boundaries

sections.scenario: A driver's app reports status changes: OPEN (online and waiting for a request), EN_ROUTE (accepted, driving to the pickup), ON_TRIP (rider on board) and OFFLINE. Utilisation, the share of online time spent with a rider on board, is a core measure of marketplace health per city and hour. The table stores only the changes, so the time in each status has to be reconstructed, and a status that crosses an hour boundary belongs partly to each hour.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns city, hour_start, drivers, open_min, en_route_min, on_trip_min, utilisation for every city and UTC hour of the report window [{{from_ts}}, {{to_ts}}) ({{hours}} hours) in which some driver of that city was online, ordered by city, hour_start. Each driver_status row starts a status that lasts until the same driver's next row in (changed_at, event_id) order or, if there is none, until {{to_ts}}. {{cap_rule}} Only the part of a status inside the window counts, split at UTC hour boundaries. OPEN, EN_ROUTE and ON_TRIP are online; OFFLINE is not. drivers is the number of distinct drivers with online time in the hour. Each _min column is the seconds spent in that status divided by 60, rounded to 2 places; utilisation = on_trip / (open + en_route + on_trip) computed from seconds and rounded to 4 places. {{window_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). hour_start is the timestamp at which the UTC hour starts. A status that lasts zero seconds contributes nothing. The sample has {{n_drivers}} drivers and {{n_rows}} status rows; a large city has tens of thousands of drivers.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical cities, drivers, statuses and window. Real driver apps have more states (arrived at pickup, paused, multiple products); this exercise uses four. The city of a driver is fixed for the day.
sections.criteria: Spans from LEAD in a deterministic order; the last status extended to the window end; statuses carried in from before the window and clipped at both ends; correct splitting at hour boundaries; distinct drivers per hour; rounding only at the end; the staleness cap at Very Hard; can discuss what utilisation does and does not tell you, and incremental computation.

clarifications.q: A driver went OPEN at 09:50 and ON_TRIP at 10:20.
clarifications.a: Ten minutes of OPEN belong to the 09:00 hour and twenty to the 10:00 hour.

clarifications.q: A driver's last row is OPEN and nothing follows.
clarifications.a: It lasts until the window ends at {{to_ts}}, unless the problem states a cap.

clarifications.q: Two rows of one driver have the same changed_at.
clarifications.a: Order by event_id: the lower one lasts zero seconds and the higher one holds from then.

clarifications.q: A status started before {{from_ts}}.
clarifications.a: It counts from {{from_ts}} on.

clarifications.q: An hour in which nobody in a city was online?
clarifications.a: Leave it out.

hints: LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY driver_id ORDER BY changed_at, event_id) gives every status its end; COALESCE the last one to the window end.
Clip each span with GREATEST and LEAST, join it to generate_series over the window's hours wherever the span overlaps the hour, and keep the overlap.
Sum seconds per status with FILTER, then divide and round only at the end.
followups: Utilisation is 0.6 in one city and 0.4 in another. What else would you need to know before calling the second city oversupplied?
A driver is online for rides and for deliveries at the same time. How would you attribute online time without counting it twice?
At millions of drivers, the hour-split join is a large fan-out. How would you compute this incrementally every hour, and what state carries over from one hour to the next?
Phones report status changes late after losing signal. How long would you wait before publishing an hour, and how would you restate it?

rules.ask: What does LEAD return for a driver's last row, and how long does that status last in your query?
You truncate each status's start to the hour. Where does the part after the next hour boundary go?
A driver went OPEN before the window started and stayed online. What does your filter give the window's first hour?
Is drivers a count of rows or of people? Think of a driver with five status changes in one hour.
Why should time beyond the cap count as offline rather than as the last known status, and what does each choice do to utilisation?

templates.title: Courier waits at restaurants, per merchant and daypart
templates.subtopic: picking the right event per order, local time zones, dayparts that wrap midnight

sections.scenario: In food delivery, a courier who arrives before the food is ready waits at the counter. Long waits waste courier time, and couriers start declining that merchant's orders. Merchants want a report per daypart in their own local time. The courier app logs ARRIVED when the courier enters the restaurant's geofence, PICKED_UP when the courier confirms the pickup, and UNASSIGNED when an order is taken away from a courier.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns merchant_id, daypart, orders, long_waits, long_wait_pct, max_wait_s for every merchant and daypart with at least {{min_orders}} measured orders, ordered by merchant_id, then daypart in the order breakfast, lunch, afternoon, dinner, late_night. An order is measured when it has a PICKED_UP event. Its pickup is its first PICKED_UP event in (event_ts, event_id) order, and the courier who picked up is that row's courier_id. The wait runs from that courier's first ARRIVED event for the order at or before the pickup, to the pickup, in seconds. The daypart comes from the local time of that arrival in the merchant's time_zone: breakfast 06:00 to before 11:00, lunch 11:00 to before 15:00, afternoon 15:00 to before 17:00, dinner 17:00 to before 22:00, and late_night 22:00 to before 06:00. A long wait is strictly more than {{n_min}} minutes ({{n_s}} seconds); long_wait_pct = ROUND(100.0 * long_waits / orders, 1). {{courier_rule}} {{data_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Orders without a pickup (cancelled) are not measured. orders counts measured orders in the group. The sample has {{n_orders}} orders and {{n_events}} courier events.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical merchants, couriers, time zones, dayparts and threshold. Geofence arrival is a proxy for walking in; real delivery apps have more signals (order ready, handed over). Timestamps are UTC instants at whole seconds.
sections.criteria: The first pickup per order and its courier; that courier's first arrival at or before the pickup; local time from the merchant's zone; dayparts that wrap midnight; strict threshold; the floor applied after measurement; reassignment and geofence re-entry handled (Hard); arrivals after pickup, duplicate pickups and pickups with no arrival handled (Very Hard); deterministic ordering by daypart rank.

clarifications.q: Which clock decides the daypart?
clarifications.a: The merchant's. Convert the arrival with AT TIME ZONE time_zone and use the local hour.

clarifications.q: The courier arrives at 10:55 local time and picks up at 11:10.
clarifications.a: Breakfast: the daypart comes from the arrival, when the wait began.

clarifications.q: Is a wait of exactly {{n_min}} minutes long?
clarifications.a: No. Long is strictly more than {{n_min}} minutes.

clarifications.q: An order was cancelled after the courier arrived.
clarifications.a: It has no pickup, so it is not measured at all.

clarifications.q: Does an order below the {{min_orders}}-order floor still count somewhere?
clarifications.a: No. A merchant's daypart with fewer measured orders is left out.

hints: Pick each order's pickup row first (DISTINCT ON (order_id)), then join back to ARRIVED events of the same courier at or before it and take the earliest.
EXTRACT(HOUR FROM arrived_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone) is the local hour. Late night wraps midnight, so test the other dayparts first and let late night take the rest.
Number the dayparts 1 to 5 for ordering and label them from the number.
followups: A long wait might be the merchant's slow kitchen or a courier who arrived too early. Which other events would tell them apart, and how would you change the metric?
A merchant's city changes to daylight saving time next week. Which dayparts are an hour longer or shorter that day, and does your query handle it?
Dispatch wants to use this to time courier arrivals per merchant. Which statistic would you give it (a mean, a percentile, something conditional on order size), and why?
A courier carries two batched orders from the same merchant: one arrival, two pickups. How does that change the wait and the count?

rules.ask: Which clock does your daypart use? A courier arriving at 12:30 in Sydney arrives at what UTC hour?
Is that the first arrival of the courier who picked up, or of anyone? What happens on a reassigned order?
The courier left and re-entered the geofence before the pickup. When did their wait start?
The average hides the tail merchants complain about. What does the share over {{n_min}} minutes tell you that the mean does not?
Which timestamp decides the daypart in your query, the arrival or the pickup, and why does it matter at 10:55?

templates.title: Nearest available drivers on a hexagonal grid
templates.subtopic: hex grids in axial coordinates, ring search, k nearest with ties

sections.scenario: A marketplace indexes the city with a grid of hexagons: every location maps to a cell, and the distance between two cells is the number of steps between neighbouring hexagons, its ring. Hexagons are convenient because all six neighbours of a cell are equally far away. Dispatch wants, for each incoming request, the nearest available drivers in rings, as the candidate list for the matching step, while location and status updates keep streaming in.
sections.problem: Implement nearest_drivers(updates, requests, k, max_ring, claim=False). Cells use axial coordinates (q, r); the distance between (q1, r1) and (q2, r2) is (|q1 − q2| + |r1 − r2| + |q1 + r1 − q2 − r2|) / 2. updates is a list of (driver_id, q, r, status) with status in 'open', 'on_trip', 'offline'. {{update_rule}} For each request (q, r), in order, return the available drivers at distance at most max_ring, nearest first, ties broken by driver_id (string comparison), at most k of them. Return a list with one list per request; a request with nobody in range gets []. {{claim_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 updates for 60 000 drivers, 15 000 requests, k ≤ 10, max_ring ≤ 10. Checking every driver for every request is too slow: the work per request should depend on the cells near it, not on the size of the fleet.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical grid, identifiers and fleet. Production hexagonal indexes (such as the open-source H3 library) add resolutions, a global coordinate system and pentagons; this exercise uses plain axial coordinates on a flat grid. Ring distance stands in for travel time, which real dispatch estimates on the road network.
sections.criteria: Correct axial distance; the last update per driver decides position and status; max_ring inclusive; ties by string id; ring-by-ring search that stops early; a cell index built once; claims removed from the index (Very Hard); a clear complexity argument; credible discussion of ETAs, update throughput and batch matching.

clarifications.q: Is a driver exactly max_ring rings away included?
clarifications.a: Yes. At most max_ring.

clarifications.q: What is the distance from (0, 0) to (2, 2)?
clarifications.a: 4, that is (2 + 2 + 4) / 2. max(|dq|, |dr|) is not the distance in axial coordinates.

clarifications.q: How are driver ids compared on a tie?
clarifications.a: As Python strings, so 'drv_100' comes before 'drv_99'.

clarifications.q: Can several drivers be in one cell?
clarifications.a: Yes, many.

clarifications.q: What if fewer than k drivers are in range?
clarifications.a: Return the ones there are.

hints: Build a dict from cell to the sorted ids of the available drivers in it, once.

Walk rings outward from the request's cell: ring 0 is the cell itself, and ring d has 6·d cells, which you reach by stepping d cells in one direction and then walking d steps along each of the six sides.
Once a finished ring brings you to k drivers, every remaining driver is farther away: stop. Only the drivers within one ring need sorting.
followups: Ring distance ignores rivers and one-way streets. How would you combine this candidate list with road-network ETAs without computing an ETA for every driver in the city?
A city sends 100 000 location updates a second. What does each update cost in your index, and how would you shard it?

With claim, each request greedily takes its nearest driver. Show a case where greedy matching gives a worse total pickup distance than matching a small batch of requests together, and how you would batch.
Downtown cells hold 50 drivers each; suburbs have none for 20 rings. How would a hierarchical grid, with coarse cells containing fine ones, change the search?

rules.ask: Work out your distance from (0, 0) to (2, 2) and to (3, −3). Which driver is nearer?
How many distance checks is that for 15 000 requests over 50 000 available drivers?
A BFS over neighbours works. What does the visited set cost per request compared with walking each ring directly?
In claim mode, what does removing a driver cost in your index, and does each cell's list stay sorted?
Do you need a heap across all candidates, or can you stop after the ring that reaches k?

templates.title: Fares from a trip's pings: surge windows, minimum fare and tolls
templates.subtopic: integer money, interval lookup with bisect, rounding once

sections.scenario: In this exercise's hypothetical pricing, a ride costs a base fare plus a per-minute and a per-kilometre charge, multiplied during surge windows when demand outstrips supply, and never less than a minimum fare; tolls are passed through to the rider at cost and a booking fee is added. After a pricing incident, the finance team needs to recompute a day of fares from each trip's GPS pings, exactly to the cent.
sections.problem: Implement fares(trips, rates, surges). Each trip is (trip_id, pings, tolls): pings are (t_s, odometer_m) with strictly increasing times, and tolls are (toll_id, t_s, cents). rates holds base, per_minute, per_km, minimum and booking_fee, all in cents. surges are (start_s, end_s, multiplier_pct): half-open windows [start_s, end_s) that never overlap, with 150 meaning 1.5×. Each interval between consecutive pings, of dt seconds and dm metres, is charged multiplier_pct / 100 × (dt × per_minute / 60 + dm × per_km / 1000) cents, using the window that contains the interval's start time (100 if none). metered is base plus the exact sum of the charges, rounded once to the nearest cent with halves rounded up; fare = max(metered, minimum). A trip's tolls are the toll events from its first ping's time to its last ping's time (inclusive), each toll_id charged once, with the cents of its first row. Return {trip_id: (fare, tolls, total)} with total = fare + booking_fee + tolls. {{window_rule}} {{odo_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 5 000 trips of 100 pings each and a few thousand surge windows. Every trip has at least one ping; all inputs are integers. The result must be exact: no floating point. Searching all windows for every interval is too slow.
sections.assumptions: The formula, rates, multipliers and windows are hypothetical and much simpler than any real pricing; real marketplaces often quote an upfront price before the trip. Here the surge multiplies time and distance only, never the base fare, the booking fee or tolls.
sections.criteria: Exact integer arithmetic with one rounding, halves up; the multiplier from the interval's start in half-open windows; base fare, booking fee and tolls never surged; the minimum applied before the booking fee and tolls; tolls charged once per toll_id (Hard) and only within the trip (Very Hard); odometer glitches handled with a high-water mark (Very Hard); sorted windows with bisect; a clear complexity argument.

clarifications.q: An interval starts exactly when a surge window ends.
clarifications.a: It is not surged: windows are half-open, and the interval takes the multiplier in effect at its start.

clarifications.q: When do I round?
clarifications.a: Once per trip, after adding the base and every charge. Halves round up: 202.5 cents is 203.

clarifications.q: Do tolls or the booking fee count towards the minimum fare?
clarifications.a: No. The minimum applies to the metered fare; the booking fee and tolls are added after it.

clarifications.q: Is the base fare surged?
clarifications.a: No.

clarifications.q: A trip has a single ping.
clarifications.a: It has no intervals: metered = base, then the minimum applies.

hints: Keep money in integers. Multiply every charge by a common denominator (for example multiplier_pct × (50·dt·per_minute + 3·dm·per_km) is the charge in units of 1/300 000 of a cent) and divide once at the end. Python's round() rounds halves to even, and floats are not exact.
Sort the windows once by start; bisect finds the only window that can contain a time.
A dict keyed by toll_id charges each toll once.
followups: Riders are quoted a price before the trip. How would you compare the quote with this metered fare, and which differences would you investigate first?
A pricing bug applied the wrong multiplier for two hours yesterday. How would you recompute, compare, and issue adjustments to riders and drivers in a way an auditor can follow?
Pings are missing for five minutes in a tunnel. How would you estimate the time and distance there, and how would you show that on the receipt?
Surge windows are per hex cell, not per city. What changes in the lookup, and what happens to an interval that crosses into another cell?

rules.ask: What does Python's round(202.5) return, and what does this fare rule require?
Where could floating point enter your fare, and can two trips with the same charges differ by a cent?
How many window checks is that for 500 000 intervals and 2 000 windows?
Which bisect finds the window for a ping exactly at a window's start, and which one for a ping exactly at its end?
The same toll_id appears twice. When is that a retry, and when could a trip really cross the same toll twice?

templates.title: Surge smoothing across neighbouring hex cells
templates.subtopic: hex k-rings, integer averaging, step limits

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace divides each city into hexagonal cells. Every interval it counts open ride requests and available drivers in each cell, and when requests outnumber drivers it raises the price multiplier there, so that more drivers head to the cell and fewer riders wait. A multiplier computed from one cell alone is noisy: a cell with one driver and three requests jumps to the cap, while the cell next door sits at 1.00x, and drivers chase the boundary. So the pricing input is smoothed over each cell's neighbourhood, capped, and not allowed to jump too far from one interval to the next.
sections.problem:
Implement smooth_surge(cells, k, cap, prev=None, max_step=None, weighted=False). cells maps a hex cell in axial coordinates (q, r) to (open_requests, available_drivers) for the interval. Cells with no data are not in it. Multipliers are integers in hundredths: 100 means 1.00x. For every cell in cells:

  1. Raw multiplier. 100 if requests are at most drivers. cap if there are no drivers and at least one request. Otherwise min(cap, 100 * requests // drivers), truncated.
  2. Smoothing. Average the raw multipliers of every cell in cells within hex distance k of this cell, itself included, and round half up to a whole hundredth. The hex distance between (q1, r1) and (q2, r2) is (|q1 − q2| + |r1 − r2| + |q1 + r1 − q2 − r2|) / 2. {{weight_rule}}
  3. Step limit. {{step_rule}}
  4. Bounds. The final multiplier is limited to the range 100 to cap.

Return a dict mapping every cell in cells to its final multiplier.
sections.constraints: About 52 000 cells and k up to 3 in the timing check; cap is at most 1 000. Something close to O(N · k²) is expected for N cells. Comparing every cell with every other cell is not fast enough. Keep the arithmetic in integers.
sections.assumptions: All counts, caps and step sizes are hypothetical, and a real pricing input uses far more signals than two counts. The grid is a flat axial hex grid, similar in spirit to open-source hexagonal indexes but without their resolutions or pentagons. Counts are non-negative integers.
sections.criteria: Correct raw multiplier, including no drivers with and without requests and truncation; correct hex distance on axial coordinates, not a square-grid distance; only cells with data averaged; round half up in integers; at Hard, a step limit from the previous value (100 when absent) applied before the bounds; at Very Hard, distance weights over the cells that have data; precomputed k-ring offsets for O(N · k²) work; a reasoned answer on spikes, incremental updates and safe testing.

clarifications.q: Do cells with no data count as 1.00x in the average?
clarifications.a: No. Only cells present in cells are averaged, so a cell at the edge of the service area averages fewer cells.

clarifications.q: Is a cell exactly k away included?
clarifications.a: Yes. The neighbourhood is every cell at distance 0 to k.

clarifications.q: How should I round?
clarifications.a: Half up, to a whole hundredth: 100.5 becomes 101. Python's round() rounds half to even, so it gives 100 there.

clarifications.q: Is the raw ratio rounded too?
clarifications.a: No, it is truncated: 7 requests and 3 drivers give 233.

clarifications.q: Which comes first, the step limit or the bounds?
clarifications.a: The step limit, then the 100 and cap bounds.

hints: On an axial grid, the cells within distance k are a fixed set of offsets (dq, dr), 3k(k + 1) + 1 of them. Build that list once.
Compute every raw multiplier once, before smoothing. Each cell then needs one dictionary lookup per offset.
With integer sum S and total weight W, (2 * S + W) // (2 * W) is S / W rounded half up.
followups: A concert ends and one cell spikes while its neighbours are calm. Your average spreads the spike over 19 cells. How would you keep a real local spike visible while still damping noise from cells with very few drivers?
The input refreshes every 30 seconds for a whole city, but only a few hundred cells change between intervals. How would you update the smoothed values without recomputing every cell?
Drivers cross a boundary between a high cell and a low cell, and the multipliers oscillate from interval to interval. What does the step limit do about that, and what else would you add?
How would you test a new smoothing rule against today's before any rider sees a price from it?

rules.ask: What does round(100.5) return in Python 3, and what would that do to a price shown to a rider?
How many distance checks is that for 52 000 cells, and how many does the list of k-ring offsets need?
Where could a float give 232.99999 instead of 233, and how do you keep the multiplier exact?
How many offsets are within distance k, and how do you generate them without duplicates or gaps?
A real hexagonal index has several resolutions and a few pentagons. What would change in your neighbour lookup?

templates.title: Inserting a new rider into a shared ride
templates.subtopic: cheapest insertion, prefix and suffix arrays, feasibility under capacity and time limits

sections.scenario: In a shared ride, riders going the same way share one car, and each is promised a pickup soon and a ride that is not much longer than a direct trip. When a new request comes in, the dispatcher looks at a candidate driver's planned sequence of pickups and drop-offs and asks: where can this rider's pickup and drop-off go so that the car never has more riders than seats, the new rider is picked up in time and does not ride too long, and nobody already promised a time is made late? Of all the places that work, it wants the one that adds the least time to the driver's route. The same routine plans long batched routes, such as a courier's multi-order run, so it must stay fast when the plan has hundreds of stops.
sections.problem:
Implement insert_rider(start, onboard, capacity, stops, pickup, dropoff, max_wait, max_ride, seats=1, dwell=0). At time 0 the car leaves start with onboard seats taken; the drop-offs of those riders are in stops without a pickup. stops is the planned sequence, each stop (rider, kind, x, y, latest, seats): a 'pickup' adds that party's seats, a 'dropoff' removes them. Travel time between two points is the Manhattan distance |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|, in seconds. {{latest_rule}} {{party_rule}}

Insert the new rider's pickup, and later their drop-off, into the sequence without reordering the planned stops. An insertion is feasible if seats taken never exceed capacity when the car leaves a stop; the car arrives at the new pickup at or before max_wait; the new rider's ride time, arrival at the drop-off minus arrival at the pickup, is at most max_ride; and every planned stop is reached by its latest. Its cost is how much later the car leaves its final stop than in the plan without the new rider (a plan with no stops finishes at 0). Return (added_seconds, pickup_index, dropoff_index), the positions of the two new stops in the new sequence, for the cheapest feasible insertion. On equal cost, return the smallest pickup_index, then the smallest dropoff_index. Return None if no insertion is feasible.
sections.constraints: Up to 600 planned stops in the timing check. There are about n²/2 candidate pairs of positions; checking each pair in constant time is expected. Rebuilding and simulating the whole route for each pair is O(n³) and too slow. All values are integers.
sections.assumptions: Locations, times and limits are hypothetical, and a street grid with Manhattan distances stands in for a road network. The planned route is feasible before the new rider is added. There are no earliest times: the car never waits for a stop. The dispatcher has already chosen this driver as a candidate.
sections.criteria: Correct arrival times, loads and slack for the plan; detours computed from the neighbouring locations, including at the end of the route; capacity checked from the pickup through the stop before the drop-off; max_wait and max_ride on arrival times; at Hard, every later planned stop within its latest after the shift it receives; at Very Hard, party sizes and dwell at every stop, including the new ones; the specified tie-break and None; O(n²) with O(1) checks per pair and a proof for each early exit; credible answers on latency budgets, concurrency and re-planning.

clarifications.q: Can the pickup and the drop-off be next to each other?
clarifications.a: Yes. Then dropoff_index is pickup_index + 1.

clarifications.q: Is latest checked on arrival or on departure?
clarifications.a: On arrival, and so is max_wait.

clarifications.q: Which loads must stay within capacity?
clarifications.a: The load when the car leaves each stop, including the new pickup. The new rider counts when the car leaves every stop between their pickup and their drop-off.

clarifications.q: Does the cost include the time spent at the new rider's own stops?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is everything that makes the final departure later.

clarifications.q: What if the new pickup is at the same place as a planned stop?
clarifications.a: It is still a separate stop in the sequence, at distance 0.

hints: Putting a stop x between locations a and b delays every later stop by the same amount: dist(a, x) + dwell + dist(x, b) − dist(a, b), or dist(a, x) + dwell at the end of the route.
Precompute, for the plan as it is, the arrival time at each stop, the load when the car leaves it, the slack latest − arrival, and the minimum slack from each stop to the end.
Fix the pickup position, then move the drop-off position forward, keeping the largest load and the smallest slack seen so far. Once either check fails, it fails for every later drop-off too.
followups: A request is checked against 40 nearby drivers within a 200 ms budget. Where does the time go, and what would you rule out before calling this function?
Travel times now come from a routing service and no longer satisfy the triangle inequality exactly. Which step of your algorithm relied on it, and what would you change?
Two requests arrive in the same second and both fit only into the same car's last seat. How does the dispatcher keep the two decisions consistent?
Cheapest insertion places one request at a time. When would you re-plan a driver's whole route instead, and what do the promises already made limit you to?

rules.ask: Riders already in the car were promised an order of stops. What happens to them, and to your running time, if you reorder?
Rebuilding and simulating each candidate is O(n) per pair. How many pairs are there for 600 stops, and what would you precompute to make each pair O(1)?
Your inner loop stops early. Prove that no later drop-off position can become feasible again.
Where exactly does your argument use it, and what breaks with travel times from a real road network?
The order of planned stops is fixed. What graph would a shortest-path search run on here, and what does it buy you over checking positions?

templates.title: Debug the trip-state reconstruction from mobile events
templates.subtopic: state machines, ordering, duplicates, illegal transitions

sections.scenario: The rider's and the driver's phones report each step of a trip: requested, accepted, arrived, started, completed or cancelled. Phones lose signal, keep events in an offline buffer and upload them later in batches, retry uploads, and have clocks that are minutes off. An analytics job rebuilds each trip's final state, its duration and a count of events that make no sense, and operations has raised several complaints about it. Trips whose driver's phone clock runs slow show up as never accepted. Trips on flaky networks show inflated illegal-event counts. Some trips that completed are reported as cancelled. Trips where the rider never came out stay "arrived" for ever. And the illegal-event alarm fires every time the mobile team raises the location sampling rate. The job below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix reconstruct_trips(events) so that it meets this specification. events is a list of dicts in delivery order, each {"event_id", "trip", "seq", "type", "device_ts"}. {{replay_rule}}

  1. Copies. A phone may upload the same event more than once. Copies share event_id and every other field. Apply each event_id once. Event ids are unique across all trips.
  2. Order. Within a trip, apply events in increasing seq, the sequence number the trip service assigned when it accepted the action. Neither the delivery order nor device_ts, the phone's clock in seconds, is reliable for ordering. Distinct events of one trip have distinct seq values.
  3. Types. The lifecycle types are requested, accepted, arrived, started, completed and cancelled. Any other type, such as location, is ignored: it changes nothing and is not counted.
  4. Transitions. From no state, only requested. requested → accepted or cancelled. accepted → arrived or cancelled. arrived → started or cancelled (a rider no-show). started → completed. completed and cancelled are final. A lifecycle event that is not allowed from the current state is illegal: count it, and leave the state unchanged.
  5. Output. {trip: {"state", "trip_seconds", "illegal"}} for every trip that appears in events. state is the last state applied, or None. trip_seconds is the device_ts of the applied completed minus the device_ts of the applied started, or None if the trip did not complete. Both come from the driver's phone, so its clock offset cancels out. illegal counts the illegal lifecycle events.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events, in O(n log n) time.
sections.assumptions: The event shapes, the transition rules and every number are hypothetical and simplified. Real trip lifecycles have more states. seq is reliable; device_ts is reliable only for differences between two events from the same phone.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; orders by seq, not by phone clocks; drops copies by event_id without counting them; never applies an illegal transition; allows a cancel after arrival; ignores non-lifecycle events; the duration comes from the applied start and completion; the fixes stay minimal and O(n log n); adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Why not order by device_ts?
clarifications.a: The rider's and the driver's phones have different clocks. Only seq is assigned in one place.

clarifications.q: Is a retransmitted copy an illegal event?
clarifications.a: No. It is the same event, so it is applied once and never counted.

clarifications.q: A driver taps "start" twice and two different events arrive. Which counts?
clarifications.a: The first one by seq. The second is illegal, because started is not allowed from started.

clarifications.q: What if a trip's requested event never arrives?
clarifications.a: Then every lifecycle event of that trip is illegal and its state is None. That is what the specification says, and the count tells operations something is missing.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Build a trip where the driver's phone runs two minutes slow, sort its events the way the code does, and read the order.
Upload one event twice. What does the second copy look like to the transition check?
After the code counts an illegal event, what happens to state?
List every state a trip can be cancelled from, and compare with the table.
followups: This now runs as a streaming job. A trip's events arrive over many minutes, some after you have already emitted its state. What do you emit, when, and how do you correct it?
Your set of seen event ids grows without limit. How would you bound it, and what can go wrong once an id has been forgotten?
The illegal-event count doubles the day after a mobile app release. How do you tell an app bug from a pipeline bug?
A phone's clock is corrected by a network time sync in the middle of a trip, so its device_ts jumps. What would you use for durations instead, and what does it cost?

rules.ask: The driver's phone runs two minutes slow. In what order do requested and accepted come out when you sort by device time?
How large does your set of seen ids grow over a day, and how would you bound it in a streaming job?
One malformed sequence from one phone: should it stop the whole job? What does the specification ask for instead?
An offline batch is uploaded twenty minutes late. What does ordering by arrival do to that trip?
A stale "accepted" retry arrives after the trip started. What does last-write-wins make of it, and how does your fix treat it?

templates.title: Fare recomputation backfill after a pricing bug
templates.subtopic: deterministic replay, versioned rules, diffs, idempotent adjustments, audit

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace prices trips from versioned pricing rules: base fare, per-minute and per-kilometre rates, minimum fares, surge multipliers, tolls and fees. Some trips are priced up front, so the rider agrees to a quoted price; others are metered on actual time and distance. A rules release contained a bug: for {{bug_window}}, trips in {{cities}} cities used the wrong per-minute rate for one vehicle class. About {{trips_affected}} trips in {{currencies}} currencies may have been priced wrongly, some too high and some too low, and driver earnings were computed from the same components. Finance, support and the city teams want to know exactly who was affected, by how much, and want the fix applied once and only once.
sections.problem: Design the backfill. Cover how you identify the affected trips; how you recompute each fare deterministically with the corrected rules from the inputs that existed at the time (the quote, the trip's measured time and distance, surge, promotions, tolls); how you produce a reviewable diff between charged and corrected amounts per trip and per component; the policy choices that decide what is adjusted for riders and for drivers, and who makes them; how adjustments are issued idempotently, in minor units, through the normal payment and earnings flows; and how every step is auditable and can be re-run.
sections.constraints: Amounts are integers in minor units of each trip's currency. A rider or a driver must never receive the same adjustment twice, even if the job is restarted. Trips refunded by support, disputed, or adjusted for another reason since the bug must not be corrected blindly. The recomputation must use the rule version that should have applied, not whatever rules are live today. Finance must be able to reconcile the totals to the ledger.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows, rates and policies are hypothetical. Each trip record keeps its pricing inputs and the identifier of the rule version used. Payments and driver earnings are separate systems that accept adjustment requests with an idempotency key.
sections.criteria: Affected trips found from rule versions and inputs, not from symptoms; deterministic recomputation from pinned inputs and the correct rule version; a component-level diff reviewed before any money moves; explicit, owned policies for overcharges, undercharges, upfront quotes and driver earnings; exclusions for trips already refunded, disputed or adjusted; idempotent adjustments with deterministic keys through the normal flows; the original amounts kept as evidence; integer minor units with the original rounding; reconciliation and an audit trail; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Do we charge riders who paid too little?
clarifications.a: That is a policy decision you should surface, not assume. Many marketplaces absorb undercharges and refund overcharges. Design for whichever policy is chosen.

clarifications.q: Does an upfront price change if the per-minute rate was wrong?
clarifications.a: The quote was computed from the rate, so the quote was wrong too. Whether the rider is owed the difference depends on whether the trip was charged the quote or the metered fare.

clarifications.q: Are driver earnings affected?
clarifications.a: Yes, where earnings are computed from the same components. Driver adjustments may follow a different policy from rider adjustments.

clarifications.q: Can the corrected rules change again during the backfill?
clarifications.a: Assume they could be revised once. Your design should make a second run cheap and safe.

clarifications.q: Who signs off?
clarifications.a: Finance and the city operations teams review the diff before any money moves.

hints: Separate three stages: recompute (pure, re-runnable, no side effects), review (a diff people can sign off), and apply (side effects, idempotent).
Pin everything a recomputation reads: the rule version, the trip's inputs, currency rounding rules and the code version. A recomputation that reads today's state is not a replay.
Give each adjustment a deterministic identity, such as the trip, the incident and the party, and use it as the idempotency key downstream.
followups: The diff shows that 3% of the trips also had a promotion applied, and the promotion was a percentage of the fare. How do you recompute those, and what does the rider see?
Midway through issuing adjustments the job crashes. Walk through the restart: what has happened downstream, and how do you know?
A second bug is found in the corrected rules after half the adjustments are out. What does your design do now?
How do you prove to finance, a quarter later, that every adjustment matches the diff that was signed off?
Some affected trips were in cities with tax rules applied to fares. What changes in the recomputation and in the adjustments?

rules.ask: The original charged amount is evidence. If you overwrite it, how do you explain a rider's receipt or reconcile last month's revenue?
What exactly is your key made of, and what happens if a second incident later affects the same trip?
Where does rounding to the minor unit happen, per component or on the total, and what does the original pricing do?
Which rule version does the replay read, and what happens if the rules change again during the backfill?
What does the rider or the driver see, and what happens if the notification goes out but the adjustment fails?

incidents: For {{bug_window}} the bug affected {{cities}} cities. The first recompute run finds 0.4% of trips whose recomputed fare differs from the charged fare in cities the bug never touched.
The adjustment job is restarted after a deploy and issues requests for trips it already processed; the payments system reports duplicate idempotency keys for 12 000 of them.
Support had already refunded some affected trips in full after complaints, and those riders would receive a second refund from the backfill.

templates.title: Assigning trips to versioned zones and geofences every day
templates.subtopic: spatial joins, cell covers, effective-dated versions, reprocessing

sections.scenario: A marketplace's analytics depend on knowing where trips start and end in business terms: which city operating zone, which pricing zone, and whether a pickup was inside a geofence such as an airport pickup area or a temporary event zone around a stadium. City teams maintain about {{zones}} zone and geofence polygons, and they change {{geofence_updates}}: new zones are added, boundaries are corrected, and event geofences exist only for a few hours. About {{daily_trips}} trips a day each have a pickup and a drop-off point, and {{late_share}} of trips reach the warehouse a day or more late because of offline phones and corrections.
sections.problem: Design the daily pipeline that assigns every trip's pickup and drop-off to zones and geofences. Cover how polygons are stored and versioned with effective dates; which version a trip is joined to (the one in effect at the trip's time); how the point-in-polygon join is made fast at this scale, for example by covering polygons with grid cells and testing exactly only near boundaries; overlapping geofences and priority rules; points on a boundary and GPS noise; late trips; what happens when a boundary correction is published for past dates; and how results stay reproducible and explainable.
sections.constraints: A trip's assignment must be explainable later: which polygon version, effective when, matched how. Corrections may be retroactive, and the business must decide whether past reports change. The daily run must finish within a few hours, and a full reprocess of a year must be possible. Downstream finance and incentive reports read these assignments.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, polygon counts and change rates are hypothetical. Polygons are stored with an id, a version, an effective-from and an effective-to time, a type (operating zone, pricing zone, airport, event) and a priority. Points are latitude and longitude from the phone, with an accuracy estimate.
sections.criteria: Polygons versioned with effective intervals and the rule for which version applies, including retroactive corrections; a cell-cover index with exact tests only near boundaries; correct handling of overlaps, boundaries and GPS accuracy with documented rules; late trips assigned with the versions in effect at their time; a targeted reprocess for corrections, with a policy for published reports; reproducible runs that record polygon versions; validation of polygon changes before use; skew and performance handled for very large polygons; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Which version applies to a trip: the one in effect at the trip's time or the latest?
clarifications.a: The one in effect at the pickup time for pickup assignments, unless a correction is declared retroactive. You decide how that is represented.

clarifications.q: Can geofences overlap?
clarifications.a: Yes. An event zone can overlap an airport's area. Each type has its own priority, and a trip can be in several geofences of different types.

clarifications.q: How precise are the points?
clarifications.a: Usually within tens of metres, worse near tall buildings and in airport garages.

clarifications.q: Who consumes the result?
clarifications.a: Pricing and incentive reports, city operations dashboards and finance. Some reports are already published when a correction arrives.

clarifications.q: Are polygons large?
clarifications.a: Most are small, but some city zones have thousands of vertices.

hints: Cover each polygon with grid cells at a fixed resolution and split them into interior cells (always inside) and boundary cells (need an exact test). Most points then need only a key lookup.
Treat the polygon table as a slowly changing dimension with effective-from and effective-to times, and join on the cell and on the time interval.
Make the output a pure function of the trips and the polygon versions it read, and record those versions with each run.
followups: An airport's boundary is corrected for the last 60 days because a new terminal opened. Which assignments change, how do you find them without reprocessing everything, and what do reports that were already published show?
One city zone has 40 000 vertices and makes the exact test slow for every point near its boundary. What would you do?
A temporary event geofence existed from 18:00 to 23:30. A trip was requested at 23:28 and picked up at 23:34. Which rule decides, and where is it written down?
GPS noise puts 2% of airport pickups just outside the airport geofence. How do you decide whether to snap them, and how would you measure the effect?
How would the same design serve a real-time assignment at request time, and how do you keep the two from disagreeing?

rules.ask: How many polygon tests does a naive join run for {{daily_trips}} trips and {{zones}} polygons, and what index would you put in front of it?
What resolution do you choose, how many cells does your largest polygon cover, and which cells still need an exact test?
A boundary changes today. What happens to last month's report if you always join with the latest polygons?
Snapping a point into the airport geofence changes who earns the airport fee. Who signs off on the tolerance, and how is it recorded?
The polygon table is small but the trips are not. What do you broadcast, and what happens when the largest polygon's cell list is skewed?

incidents: A city team publishes a corrected airport boundary effective from 45 days ago, and the incentive report for that airport has already been paid out to drivers.
Geofences change {{geofence_updates}}. One event geofence is published with its effective-to time earlier than its effective-from time, and the daily run silently assigns no trips to it.

{{late_share}} of trips arrive a day or more late; on one day a mobile backlog delivers three days of trips at once, and the late trips are joined with today's polygons instead of the ones in effect when they happened.

templates.title: Trips, shared-ride legs and fares that change after the ride
templates.subtopic: vehicle trip versus rider leg, fare components, post-trip adjustments and tips

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace completes about {{daily_trips}} trips a day, priced in {{currencies}} currencies. In this scenario a rider is shown an upfront price when requesting; the price is built from components (a base amount, time and distance, a dynamic-pricing adjustment, a booking fee, airport or toll surcharges, a promotion and taxes), and the driver's earnings are calculated separately from what the rider pays. About {{shared_share}} of vehicle trips are shared: several riders, each with their own pickup, drop-off and price, ride in one vehicle at once, and the driver is paid for the vehicle trip. After the ride, things change: a rider can add a tip for up to {{tip_window_days}} days, support can adjust a fare after a route complaint, a cleaning fee can be charged, and a promotion can be reversed when a payment fails. Rider receipts, driver earnings statements and the finance team's gross bookings and take rate must all agree.
sections.problem: Design the data model from the trip service to the analytical facts. Cover: the vehicle trip, the rider legs on it (shared or not) and the keys between them; the fare at its proper grain, with components as typed lines and the price version that produced them; driver earnings as their own lines on the vehicle trip; how post-trip changes (tips, adjustments, refunds, fees, promotion reversals) are recorded without rewriting what a rider or driver already saw; and the facts with their grains that answer "gross bookings and take rate by city and day", "driver earnings per online hour", "adjustments by reason and city" and "tips as a share of fares". Write one definition of gross bookings and one of take rate that finance can use.
sections.constraints: Money is stored as integers in each currency's minor unit, together with its currency; amounts in different currencies are never added without an explicit, dated conversion. A rider's receipt and a driver's statement, once issued, change only through new lines that both can see. Tips belong to the driver and are never part of the marketplace's revenue in this scenario. The state of a trip's money at any past time must be reconstructable.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares, the tip window and the currency count are hypothetical, as are the fare components and the rule that tips go wholly to drivers. A shared trip's rider prices are set when each rider is matched and need not sum to the driver's earnings. Pricing rules themselves are out of scope; only their version is recorded.
sections.criteria: Vehicle trip and rider leg as separate grains with explicit keys; fare components and earnings as typed, signed lines with the price version; post-trip changes appended as lines that both receipt and statement can see; tips kept out of revenue; money as integer minor units with a currency and a known exponent; written definitions of gross bookings and take rate; facts at stated grains with a policy for late tips in closed months; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is the shared trip one trip or several?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but both the driver's vehicle trip and each rider's leg must be identifiable. The driver sees one trip; each rider sees their own.

clarifications.q: Can the final price differ from the upfront price?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this scenario, when the rider changes the destination or the route differs greatly. Record both and why they differ.

clarifications.q: Which date does a tip count on?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say whether finance reports tips on the trip date or the tip date, and how a month that has closed handles a late tip.

clarifications.q: Who pays a cancellation fee?
clarifications.a: The rider, when they cancel after a grace period; the driver receives part of it. A trip that never started can still carry money.

clarifications.q: Are all currencies two-decimal?
clarifications.a: No. Some currencies have no minor unit and a few have three decimals.

hints: Separate the vehicle trip (driver, vehicle, route, timestamps) from the rider leg (rider, pickup, drop-off, price). A non-shared trip is a vehicle trip with one leg.
Treat each receipt and each earnings statement as a small ledger: typed, signed lines that are appended, never edited. Current totals are sums.
Record the currency's minor-unit exponent once in a currency dimension, not in each amount column's code path.
followups: Walk one shared trip with three riders, one of whom changes the destination, through your tables. What does each rider's receipt show, and what does the driver's statement show?
A tip arrives {{tip_window_days}} days after the trip, in a month already closed for finance. Which rows are created, which reports change, and which do not?
Define gross bookings and take rate precisely. Which line types are in each, and how are tips, tolls, taxes and refunds treated?
Support refunds part of a fare after a route complaint, and the driver's earnings are not reduced. How does the take rate for that trip look, and is that what finance wants?
At {{daily_trips}} trips a day, which facts do you keep at line grain, which at trip or leg grain, and how do you keep the daily refresh cheap when tips trickle in for {{tip_window_days}} days?

rules.ask: A tip, a cleaning fee and a partial refund arrive in the week after the trip. Where do they go if the fare is one column, and how does the receipt from the day of the trip stay the same?
A city prices in a currency with no minor unit and another in a three-decimal currency. How are amounts stored, and how does a report avoid being off by a factor of 100 or 1,000?
Three riders' fares are joined to the vehicle trip and its driver earnings. What does SUM(driver_earnings) return for that trip, and how does your model prevent it?
The driver downloaded last week's statement before a fare adjustment. How do you show them what changed and why, without the old statement disagreeing with the new one?
Which rate and which date convert a trip's money, and what happens to last month's gross bookings when a rate is corrected?

incidents: Tips that arrive days after the trip are attached by updating the trip's fact row. Driver earnings statements already sent no longer match the warehouse, and the tips-share-of-fares metric for last month drifts every day for {{tip_window_days}} days.

A dashboard joins rider legs to vehicle trips and sums driver earnings: for the {{shared_share}} of trips that are shared, earnings are counted once per rider, and earnings per online hour look far too high in the busiest cities.

One market's currency has no minor unit, but a new pipeline divides every amount by 100. Its gross bookings fall a hundredfold on the global dashboard, and nobody notices for two days because that market is small.

templates.title: Driver onboarding and document compliance, city by city, with full history
templates.subtopic: effective-dated requirement rules, document versions, compliance intervals, audit

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing and delivery marketplace works with about {{drivers}} active drivers and couriers across {{cities}} cities. Before someone can go online, and for as long as they stay online, they must hold valid documents, and the set depends on the city and the product: a driver's licence, a vehicle registration, commercial insurance, a vehicle inspection, a city permit, a background check, and for delivery by bicycle almost none of these. There are {{document_types}} document types in all. Each document is submitted (often as a photo), checked automatically and sometimes by a reviewer, and carries an expiry date. Cities change their rules with effective dates: a new inspection requirement, a shorter renewal period. In this scenario a driver whose document expires has {{grace_days}} days of grace before they are blocked from going online. Regulators and the safety team must be able to ask, for any past trip, "was this driver compliant, under the rules then in force, at that moment?"
sections.problem: Design the data model for requirements, documents and compliance. Cover: requirement rules per city and product as effective-dated versions; document submissions, their review decisions (automated and manual, with reasons) and the extracted fields (number, issuer, expiry); compliance as intervals per driver, city and product derived from the two; the onboarding funnel (sign-up, documents submitted, approved, first trip); and the facts that answer "time from sign-up to first trip by city and week", "documents expiring in the next 30 days", "reviews per reviewer and outcome", and "trips taken while not compliant" (which should be none). Say where document images live and who can see what.
sections.constraints: Rules are never edited in place: a change is a new version with an effective time. A decision on a document is never deleted; a later decision supersedes it. Compliance at any past instant must be reproducible from what was known then, and separately from what is known now. Document images and personal fields are visible only to roles that need them; the analytical warehouse keeps no images. Expiry is evaluated in the city's local time.
sections.assumptions: Driver counts, city counts, document types and grace periods are hypothetical, and so are the rules. A driver can be onboarded in more than one city and for more than one product. Background-check results arrive from an external provider and can take days.
sections.criteria: Effective-dated rule versions per city and product; documents, extracted fields and append-only decisions with reasons; compliance as derived half-open intervals with grace, transitions and revocations; trips joined to intervals by time; two time axes for known-then versus known-now; local-time expiry with an explicit time zone; images separated with access control and retention; funnel and audit facts at stated grains; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a new rule apply to drivers who are already active?
clarifications.a: Yes, from its effective date, unless the rule says existing drivers have a transition period. Model both.

clarifications.q: Can a document be approved and later found invalid?
clarifications.a: Yes, after an audit. The approval stays on record and a new decision revokes it from a stated time.

clarifications.q: Is a document's expiry a date or an instant?
clarifications.a: A date printed on the document. You decide which local instant it ends, and in which time zone.

clarifications.q: Does one document serve several cities?
clarifications.a: A licence can; a city permit cannot. Requirements reference document types, and a document can satisfy requirements in several cities.

clarifications.q: What happens to the data when a driver leaves?
clarifications.a: Personal data is deleted after a retention period; the facts needed for safety audits are kept in a form you describe.

hints: Keep three things apart: what was required (rule versions), what was presented and decided (documents and decisions), and the derived compliance intervals.
Compliance is an interval table: (driver, city, product, valid_from, valid_to, reason). A trip joins to it with a half-open time condition.
"Known then" versus "known now" is two time axes: when something was true, and when the system recorded it.
followups: Write the derivation of compliance intervals for one driver whose insurance expires, is renewed four days later, and whose city adds an inspection requirement in between. Show the intervals with a {{grace_days}}-day grace.
An audit revokes an approval of a licence made three months ago. Which past trips become "taken while not compliant", and how does the report distinguish "known then" from "known now"?
A city adds a requirement with a transition period for existing drivers. How do the rule version and the intervals represent it?
At {{drivers}} drivers and {{cities}} cities, how often do you recompute intervals, and what event triggers a recompute for one driver instead of everyone?
A driver asks for their data to be deleted. What is removed, what is kept for safety audits, and in what form?

rules.ask: A regulator asks whether a driver was compliant at 21:40 on a date eight months ago. Your flag says true today. How do you answer?
The document says it expires on a date. In a city twelve hours ahead of UTC, at which instant is the driver blocked, and who decides?
A city shortens its renewal period from next month. Is the old rule overwritten? How does an audit of last month's trips see the old one?
Who can open the licence photo, how long is it kept, and does any of it reach the warehouse?
Show the two queries: compliant under what we knew at the time, and compliant under what we know now. Which one does a regulator ask for?

incidents: A city's rule was corrected by editing the existing rule row instead of adding a version. The safety team's monthly audit now reports hundreds of past trips as non-compliant that were compliant under the rule in force at the time.

The nightly expiry job evaluates dates in the server's UTC day. Drivers in cities far east of UTC are blocked several hours late; with a {{grace_days}}-day grace the window is shifted by most of a day, and some trips run on expired insurance.

Automatic extraction read some expiry dates in month/day order where the document uses day/month. Across {{document_types}} document types the share is small, but some drivers stayed online with expired documents and others were blocked with valid ones.

templates.title: Hex cells, zones and geofences that change over time
templates.subtopic: hierarchical hex grid, versioned polygons, effective dating, point-in-zone assignment

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing and delivery marketplace describes places in two ways. For pricing, supply and demand it uses a hierarchical hexagonal grid, such as the open-source H3 system: the earth is divided into hexagonal cells at 16 resolutions, each cell has about seven children at the next finer resolution, the children do not cover their parent exactly, and each resolution also has twelve pentagons. Here the base resolution is {{base_resolution}}. For operations it uses polygons: city boundaries, pricing zones, airport pickup areas with their own rules, and short-lived event geofences around a stadium for a concert night. There are about {{geofences}} active zones and geofences, and operations edits about {{zone_edits_per_week}} a week: a zone is redrawn, split in two, merged, or an event geofence is created for a few hours. The platform assigns about {{daily_points}} location points a day (pings, pickups, drop-offs) to cells and zones, and analysts compare metrics for a zone across months in which its boundary changed.
sections.problem: Design the geospatial reference model. Cover: cells (id, resolution, parent) and what "parent" means when children do not nest exactly; zones and geofences with types, owners and versioned geometries; effective dating (valid from and to) and, separately, when each version was recorded; a derived mapping from base-resolution cells to zone versions, with the rule used for cells on a boundary; precedence when zones overlap (an airport pickup area inside a pricing zone inside a city); how a point is assigned for pricing (fast, approximate) and for an airport rule or a tax boundary (exact); and how metrics are compared across versions of a zone.
sections.constraints: A zone version is immutable once published; a correction is a new version. Any historical point or trip can be re-assigned to the zones that were in force at its time, and the report says which versions it used. Cell ids are stable and meaningful; zone ids survive redraws while version ids change. A city lookup must answer in milliseconds; an exact polygon test is allowed only where the rule requires it.
sections.assumptions: Counts, edit rates and the base resolution are hypothetical; the grid facts above describe the open-source system in general terms (check current docs). Geometries are stored in one coordinate reference system (longitude and latitude). Event geofences carry a time window as well as a geometry.
sections.criteria: Grid, zone catalogue and immutable zone versions separated; valid time and recorded time kept apart; an explicit boundary-cell rule and an exact test only where a rule needs it; precedence for overlapping types; precomputed cell-to-version mappings with stable cell ids; parent rollups treated as approximate; a stated policy for backdating and for "as it was" versus "as it is" reporting; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Does a zone equal a set of cells?
clarifications.a: Approximately. You decide the rule for boundary cells (cell centre inside the polygon, any overlap, or majority of area) and when an exact polygon test overrides it.

clarifications.q: Can two zones of the same type overlap?
clarifications.a: Pricing zones must not; geofences of different types can, and an airport area overrides its pricing zone for pickups.

clarifications.q: What happens to history when a zone is split?
clarifications.a: The old zone's last version ends; two new zones (or the old one and a new one) start. Analysts still want a continuous series where it makes sense.

clarifications.q: Can a version be backdated?
clarifications.a: Operations sometimes asks for it. Decide whether you allow it and how reports that already used the old version find out.

clarifications.q: Are cells at a coarser resolution exact unions of base cells?
clarifications.a: No. Rolling up base cells to a coarser parent is approximate at the edges.

hints: Separate the grid (static, computed by a library), the zone catalogue (zone id, type, owner), and zone versions (geometry, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at).
Precompute cell to zone-version mappings per version at the base resolution; a lookup is then an equality join on the cell id plus a time condition.
For metrics across a redraw, decide between "as it was" (each period with its own version) and "as it is" (re-assign history to the current geometry), and label which.
followups: A pricing zone is split in two. Show the rows in the zone, version and mapping tables before and after, and how a monthly trend for the old zone is drawn.
A pickup lands in a base-resolution cell that straddles the airport boundary. How does the pricing lookup assign it, and when does the airport rule run an exact test?
Estimate the size of the cell-to-zone mapping at resolution {{base_resolution}} for a large city, and how it grows if you move one resolution finer.
A version was published with a valid_from two weeks in the past. Which facts must be recomputed, and how do you tell their consumers?
With {{daily_points}} points a day, where does the point-to-cell and cell-to-zone assignment happen, and what is stored with each point so it never has to be repeated?

rules.ask: Why might a hexagonal grid suit pricing and neighbour lookups better than rectangles, and what does a geohash give you that a hex grid does not?
The children of a cell do not cover it exactly. What does a zone metric computed from coarser parents count twice or miss at the edges?
An exact point-in-polygon test for every one of the points is expensive. Which points need it, and how do the others avoid it?
Is valid_from the time the boundary applies or the time it was recorded? Show what happens when operations backdates a version.
Last month's airport pickup report was computed with the old boundary. After the geometry is overwritten, can you reproduce that report?

incidents: A redrawn pricing zone was published with a valid_from in the past. The nightly job re-assigned the previous month's trips, and city reports for a month already closed changed without notice.

A dashboard computed zone metrics by rolling base resolution {{base_resolution}} cells up to their coarser parents. Because children do not nest exactly, trips near zone edges were counted in two zones or none, and the totals stopped matching the city's.

An event geofence around a stadium was created without an end time. Its pickup rules stayed active for nine days, and about {{zone_edits_per_week}} weekly edits made it hard to find which change caused it.

templates.title: Delivery orders, batched courier trips and refunds by item
templates.subtopic: order items with modifiers, many-to-many orders and courier trips, item-level refunds, cost allocation

sections.scenario: A food and grocery delivery marketplace takes about {{daily_orders}} orders a day from {{merchants}} merchants. An order holds items, each with a quantity and modifiers (a size, extra toppings, a substitution preference); grocery items can be substituted or found out of stock while being picked. Couriers deliver, and about {{batched_share}} of orders are batched: one courier trip picks up two or more orders, sometimes from different merchants, and drops them off in a sequence. Couriers are paid per trip, with components for distance, time and each extra stop. Customers pay item prices, a delivery fee, a service fee and sometimes a small-order fee, minus promotions that are funded by the marketplace or by the merchant. About {{refund_share}} of orders get a refund, usually for one or two items (missing, wrong, damaged), and whether the merchant or the marketplace bears it depends on the reason.
sections.problem: Design the data model from the order and dispatch systems to the analytical facts. Cover: orders, order items and modifiers with the menu or catalogue version they were ordered from; substitutions and out-of-stock events; courier trips, their stops and the many-to-many link between trips and orders (including an order re-assigned to a second courier); money as typed lines for customer charges, merchant payouts, courier pay and promotions with their funder; item-level refunds with a reason and a liable party. Define the facts and grains that answer "refund rate by merchant and item", "delivery cost per order", "time from merchant ready to drop-off, per order, for batched and single orders", and "merchant payout per week".
sections.constraints: Money is stored as integers in minor units with a currency. Refunded quantity for an item line never exceeds its ordered quantity, and refunded amount never exceeds what was charged for it. An item ordered last month is reported under what it was then, even if the menu changed. Courier pay is never shown to merchants, and customer details are never shown to couriers after delivery.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and fee types are hypothetical. In this scenario courier pay is set per trip, not per order. A merchant can edit its menu at any time; item ids may be reused by the merchant for a different dish.
sections.criteria: Order item as the grain for money and refunds, with modifiers and a menu snapshot; substitutions and out-of-stock events kept; courier trips and orders linked many-to-many through stops; courier pay stored once and allocated by a stated rule; typed money lines with funder and liable party; refund invariants enforced with idempotency; delivery-time definitions per audience; visibility rules for merchants and couriers; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can an order be split across couriers?
clarifications.a: Rarely, for a large grocery order. More often an order is re-assigned when a courier cancels; both trips are recorded.

clarifications.q: Which time does "delivery time" start from?
clarifications.a: Define it. The customer sees time from placing the order; merchants are judged from the time they marked it ready.

clarifications.q: Who bears a refund for a missing item?
clarifications.a: In this scenario the merchant for missing or wrong items it packed, the marketplace for damage in transit. The liable party is recorded per refund line.

clarifications.q: Is a substitution a new item line?
clarifications.a: Your choice. The customer is charged for what was delivered, and the merchant's item metrics need both what was ordered and what was sent.

clarifications.q: Can a refund be issued twice for the same item?
clarifications.a: It must not be. Refunds arrive from the app and from support chat.

hints: Snapshot the item name, price and modifiers onto the order item line from the menu version; never join an old order to the current menu for its name or price.
A courier trip and an order are many-to-many through a stop table (trip, stop sequence, order, pickup or drop-off, times).
Courier cost per order needs an allocation rule written down (by stops, by distance, equal split); the trip's pay itself is stored once.
followups: Walk a batched trip with two orders from two merchants, where one item in the second order is refunded. Which rows exist, and what are the delivery cost and refund cost per order?
A merchant reuses an item id for a different dish. How does your model keep last month's refund rate for the old dish correct?
Write the refund invariant as a check. Where does it run, and what happens to a support refund that would break it?
Choose the courier-cost allocation rule for batched orders and justify it. How does the cost per order change when {{batched_share}} of orders are batched?
At {{daily_orders}} orders a day, which facts are kept at item grain and which at order or trip grain, and how are late refunds folded in?

rules.ask: One courier trip carries three orders. Joined to orders, what does SUM(courier_pay) return, and what does your cost per order show?
The merchant renamed and repriced a dish last week. What do last month's item-level reports show if the order joins to the menu?
The app and a support agent both refund the same missing drink. What stops the second refund, and what does the item-level refund rate show if it slips through?
In a batched trip the second order waits while the first is dropped off. Whose delivery time includes that wait, and is the merchant judged on it?
A promotion is funded half by the merchant and half by the marketplace. How does that split appear in the merchant's payout and in the marketplace's take rate?

incidents: A cost-per-order dashboard joined each courier trip's pay to every order on the trip. For the {{batched_share}} of orders that are batched, delivery cost was counted several times, and batching looked more expensive than single orders.
A merchant chain reused item ids for a new menu. Refund rates for its old dishes jumped, because new refunds were attributed to old item names joined from the menu.

The app and support chat both issued refunds for the same missing items for a few hours. About {{refund_share}} of orders are refunded normally; that day some orders were refunded more than their charge, and merchant payouts were reduced twice.

templates.title: Surge exposure per city and local hour
templates.subtopic: half-open range join, default multiplier, local time zones, fan-out, weighted shares
