sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace prices each request with a dynamic multiplier. In this exercise's model, when demand outruns supply in a zone, the pricing system opens a surge window for that zone: surge_windows holds windows per zone_id with a multiplier, each covering starts_at up to but not including ends_at; windows of one zone never overlap, adjacent windows can touch, and a window may set exactly 1.00x. ride_requests holds each request with its city_id and zone_id, and trips holds each match of a request to a driver with its status (completed, rider_cancelled or driver_cancelled). {{trip_rule}} Each city reports in its own time zone, from cities.time_zone; the cities here are {{city_list}}. The marketplace health team wants to know how exposed riders were to surge pricing, per city and local hour: as a share of requests, and weighted by the trips that actually completed.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query for the local report date {{report_date}} that returns city_id, local_hour, requests, surged_requests, request_surge_share, completed_trips, surged_completed_trips, completed_surge_share, ordered by city_id, local_hour. A request belongs to the local date and hour of its requested_at in its city's time zone; local_hour is the start of that hour as a local timestamp without time zone (for example {{report_date}} 08:00:00). Only requests on the report date count. A request's multiplier is that of the window of its zone with starts_at <= requested_at < ends_at, or 1.00 when no window is in force; it is surged when the multiplier is above 1.00. requests counts the hour's requests and surged_requests the surged ones. completed_trips counts the hour's requests that have a completed trip (a completed trip counts in the hour of its request, whenever it ended), and surged_completed_trips the surged ones among them. request_surge_share is surged_requests / requests and completed_surge_share is surged_completed_trips / completed_trips, both rounded to 4 decimal places; completed_surge_share is NULL when completed_trips is 0. Return only (city, hour) rows with at least {{min_requests}} requests.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The session time zone is UTC. The sample has {{requests_n}} requests, {{windows_n}} surge windows and {{trips_n}} trips; production has tens of millions of requests a day across hundreds of cities, and windows change every few minutes.
sections.assumptions: The schema, zones, windows, multipliers, requests and trips are hypothetical, and the cities' names and time zones are labels only. No listed time zone changes its UTC offset on the report date. A zone belongs to one city. Fares and amounts are out of scope.
sections.criteria: Each request priced by a LEFT JOIN on its zone with a half-open interval and a 1.00 default; surge as strictly above 1.00; trips reduced to one completed flag per request before counting; local hour and local date from the city's time zone; completed trips counted in the request's hour; shares rounded as stated with NULL for an empty denominator; the floor applied in HAVING; deterministic order; can explain why hourly shares are not averaged, why the quoted multiplier should be stored on the request, and how a repeated local hour behaves.

clarifications.q: Is a request at exactly ends_at priced by that window?
clarifications.a: No. Windows are half-open: starts_at <= requested_at < ends_at. A request at exactly starts_at is priced by the window.

clarifications.q: What about a request when no window is open for its zone?
clarifications.a: It is priced at 1.00x: not surged, but it is a request and stays in the denominator.

clarifications.q: Does a 1.00x window count as surge?
clarifications.a: No. Surge means strictly above 1.00x.

clarifications.q: In which hour does a completed trip count?
clarifications.a: In the hour of its request, even if the trip ended in a later hour or on the next day.

clarifications.q: What if an hour has requests but nothing completed?
clarifications.a: Keep the row if it meets the floor, with completed_trips 0 and a NULL completed_surge_share.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines the report date?
clarifications.a: Each city's own, the same one that defines its hours.

hints: Price each request first: LEFT JOIN the window of its zone with a half-open range condition, and COALESCE the multiplier to 1.00.
Reduce trips to one "completed" flag per request before joining (EXISTS, or a DISTINCT list of completed request ids). Joining requests to all their trips multiplies them.
requested_at AT TIME ZONE c.time_zone gives the local wall-clock time; truncate it to the hour, and cast it to a date for the report-date filter.
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) counts a subset; NULLIF(x, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL.
followups: The team rolls the hourly shares up to a day per city. Why is the average of the hourly shares wrong, and what do you compute instead?
Operations later corrects a window that stayed open by mistake. Should this report recompute the multiplier from the windows, or use the multiplier each rider was quoted? Which table would you add?
On a day when a city's clocks fall back, one local hour happens twice. What does your query return for it, and what should the report show?
At production scale, how do you make the range join to windows cheap, and how would you serve this metric for every city every few minutes?

rules.ask: BETWEEN includes both ends. A request arrives exactly at one window's ends_at, which is also the next window's starts_at. Which multiplier does it get under your join, and how many rows does it produce?
Which requests disappear when no window is open for their zone at that moment, and what happens to the denominator of the share?
A city is UTC+5:30. Which UTC hour bucket holds its 08:00–09:00 local hour, and which local date does a request at 20:00 UTC on the report date belong to?
Average over which rows? After joining trips, a re-matched request appears several times. What does that do to your share?
COUNT(DISTINCT request_id) fixes the requests column after a join to trips. Are surged_requests and the completed counts protected the same way?
Is a request priced at exactly 1.00x exposed to surge? What does your comparison count for a window that sets 1.00x?

incidents: After a pricing incident, operations shortened a surge window that had stayed open by mistake. This report, recomputed from the corrected windows, now shows those riders as unsurged although their receipts show a surge; the multiplier each request was quoted was never stored with it.

A first version of this report bucketed hours in UTC. For a city at UTC+5:30 every local hour was split across two bars and its local midnight hour landed on the previous day, and the city team stopped trusting the numbers for a week.

templates.title: Live supply and demand per hex cell, every 30 seconds, as a pricing input
templates.subtopic: geospatial aggregation, windowing, freshness as a contract

sections.scenario: A ride-hailing marketplace covers its cities with a hexagonal grid (an open-source hierarchical hex system, with cells a few hundred metres across at the finest level used here). At peak about {{drivers}} drivers are online at once, and each driver app sends a location and status ping (offline, open, en route to pickup, on trip) roughly every {{ping_seconds}} seconds. Riders open the app and request trips, at a peak of about {{requests}} requests per second worldwide; each app open with a destination produces a price quote. Every 30 seconds, the pricing service needs, for every active cell, a fresh view of supply (drivers who could take a new trip in or near the cell soon) and demand (app opens with intent, and requests) to compute its multiplier.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that produces this supply and demand map. Define precisely what counts as supply and as demand in a cell for a 30-second interval; describe ingestion from the apps, the aggregation (including neighbouring cells), how the result is published to the pricing service, and what pricing does when the map is late. Say how the same data is kept for analysis and for later replay.
sections.constraints: The map for a cell must never be older than {{staleness}} when pricing reads it; if it is, pricing must know and fall back. A driver must be counted at most once per interval, however many pings they send. Pings arrive out of order and some are duplicated; driver apps buffer pings while offline and send them later. Pricing reads must be p99 under 10 ms. Each city's map must keep working if another region of the platform is down.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and latencies are hypothetical. Each ping carries a driver id, the app's timestamp, a sequence number per driver session, latitude and longitude, accuracy, and the status. Requests and app opens arrive on a separate stream from the rider apps.
sections.criteria: Precise definitions of supply (distinct drivers by state, with soon-available counted separately) and demand (requests and intent-bearing app opens) per cell and interval; per-driver ordered processing with dedup by session sequence and a current-state store; cell aggregation with sparse-cell handling (parent cells or neighbour smoothing with boundaries respected); an explicit lateness policy and a published freshness timestamp; a fast keyed read path for pricing with a defined fallback when stale; regional isolation and state rebuild on failover; every interval stored for analysis and replay with versioned definitions; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a driver on a trip that ends in two minutes count as supply?
clarifications.a: Product wants "soon-available" supply counted separately from open drivers. You define "soon" and say how you know the trip will end.

clarifications.q: Is demand measured by requests or by app opens?
clarifications.a: Both are wanted. Requests undercount demand when prices are high, because some riders do not request.

clarifications.q: How precise is the location?
clarifications.a: Usually within tens of metres, but in dense downtowns and near tall buildings it can be off by hundreds of metres.

clarifications.q: Does pricing need history?
clarifications.a: Only the latest map. Analysts and the replay team want every interval kept.

clarifications.q: Can the cell size vary?
clarifications.a: You may aggregate to coarser parent cells where data is sparse; say how you decide.

hints: Supply is a count of distinct drivers in a state at a moment, not a count of pings. Keep each driver's latest known state and count from that.
Key the stream so each driver's pings are processed in order by one worker, then aggregate by cell in a second stage.
Decide what pricing does when a city's map is stale before you design the fast path. The fallback is part of the contract.
followups: A driver's pings arrive 20 seconds late after a tunnel. In which interval and cell is that driver counted, and why?
A cell has two drivers and no requests in most intervals. How do you keep the multiplier from swinging on noise?
One city's partition falls three minutes behind during a stadium event. What does pricing see in that city, and what does it do?
How would you show, a week later, the exact supply and demand values that a particular price quote used?
Product wants a 10-second interval for the busiest 20 cities. What changes, and what does it cost?

rules.ask: What is the partition key for pings, and how does that choice behave when one city's demand spikes during a concert?
Do you need an approximate distinct count here, or can you count exactly? How many drivers can be in one cell at once?
Smoothing across neighbouring cells blurs a sharp boundary such as a river with one bridge. How do you keep the airport queue from leaking supply into the motorway next to it?
Waiting for late pings makes the map older. How long do you wait before you publish an interval, and what happens to pings that arrive after it?
The node holding one city's latest map restarts. What does pricing read for the next 30 seconds?

incidents: A driver app release on one mobile platform starts sending two pings every {{ping_seconds}} seconds instead of one. Within an hour, supply in every city looks about 40% higher and multipliers fall citywide.

A stadium concert ends; requests in six cells rise twentyfold within ten minutes. The partition that carries that city falls three minutes behind, so the map pricing reads there is older than {{staleness}}.
A GPS fault at an airport makes several hundred waiting drivers appear in a cell across the motorway from the official waiting lot, and the airport cell shows almost no supply.
One region of the platform goes down for 40 minutes; cities whose apps are served from it are moved to another region, which starts with no driver state for them.

templates.title: Trip lifecycle event pipeline from out-of-order, offline mobile events
templates.subtopic: state machines at scale, ordering, late and duplicate events

sections.scenario: A marketplace completes about {{trips}} rides and deliveries a day. Each produces about {{events_per_trip}} lifecycle events from three sources: the rider app, the driver or courier app, and the marketplace's own services (requested, matched, driver arrived, trip started, stop added, destination changed, trip ended, cancelled, fare finalised, tip added). Driver and courier apps buffer events while they have no signal and send them later, sometimes up to {{offline_hours}} hours afterwards. The same event can arrive twice, and the two apps can disagree (the rider app says the trip was cancelled while the driver app says it started). {{consumers}} downstream teams depend on the trip's state: earnings, fares and receipts, safety, support tooling, marketplace analytics and the city metrics.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that turns these events into one authoritative state and history per trip. Cover ingestion, ordering, deduplication, the state machine and what happens to illegal transitions, how conflicts between sources are resolved, how corrections after a trip ends are published, and what downstream consumers receive (a current-state table, a change stream, or both) with what guarantees.
sections.constraints: Support tools must see a trip's current state within 5 seconds of the event reaching the platform. A trip's state may change after it ends (a fare adjustment, a late tip, a cancellation fee reversed by support); every change must be traceable to the event that caused it. Device clocks can be wrong by minutes. Events must never be silently dropped, even when they cannot be applied.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and timings are hypothetical. Every event carries a trip id, an event type, a source, a client-generated event id, the device or server timestamp, a per-device sequence number, and the time the platform received it.
sections.criteria: An immutable event log keyed by trip with dedup on event id and on (device session, sequence); state derived deterministically from ordered events with per-event-type source authority; explicit handling of illegal transitions (held, retried after more events arrive, or recorded with a reason, never dropped); late events and post-trip corrections as versioned changes; a change stream plus a current-state table with clear guarantees and a version per trip; rebuild and restatement with correction semantics for consumers; reconciliation that accounts for every event and checks consumers; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which source wins when the apps disagree?
clarifications.a: You define the rule. Some events are only authoritative from one side, such as "trip ended" from the driver app, "cancelled by rider" from the rider app, and fare finalisation from the server.

clarifications.q: Can a trip go back to an earlier state?
clarifications.a: Not normally, but support can reverse a cancellation or a completion with an explicit correction event.

clarifications.q: Do downstream teams need every intermediate state?
clarifications.a: Safety and analytics want the full history; earnings and receipts want the final state and every later correction.

clarifications.q: How late is too late?
clarifications.a: Nothing is too late to store. You decide which late events still change state and which are recorded only.

clarifications.q: Is ordering by device timestamp safe?
clarifications.a: Within one device session the sequence number is reliable; timestamps across devices are not.

hints: Separate the immutable event log from the derived state. State is a pure function of the ordered events for a trip, so it can always be rebuilt.
Order within a source by its sequence number; merge sources with explicit authority rules per event type rather than by timestamp alone.
Give each trip a version that increases with every applied change; consumers can then process changes idempotently and in order.
followups: A "trip ended" event arrives four hours after the trip, while the trip shows "cancelled by rider" from the rider app. What does the state become, and what do earnings and receipts receive?
How do you handle an event your state machine says is illegal, such as "trip started" before "matched"?
A bug in state derivation is found that affected the last 10 days. How do you rebuild state and tell consumers what changed?
Partitioning by trip id puts each trip's events in order, but some consumers want everything for one driver in order. How do you serve both?
How do you prove each day that every event received was either applied or recorded as rejected with a reason?

rules.ask: A driver's phone clock is 9 minutes fast. Show me one trip where ordering by device time gives the wrong final state.
Which part of your pipeline actually gives exactly-once effects, and what do consumers do when they see a change twice anyway?
Who looks at the rejected events, how often, and what makes one go back into the pipeline?
A consumer reads the current-state table every five minutes and misses a state that lasted two minutes. Does that matter for them? What should they read instead?
Rebuilding ten days of state produces changes for 3% of trips. Which consumers must receive those changes, and how do they know they are corrections rather than new trips?

incidents: A mobile network outage in one large city leaves many driver apps offline for up to {{offline_hours}} hours; when it ends, the buffered events from 40,000 trips arrive within ten minutes, many for trips the rider app already reported as finished.
A driver app release generates a new event id each time it retries a send, so "trip ended" arrives two or three times with different ids for about 2% of trips. Earnings shows some trips twice.
A server deploy emits "fare finalised" before "trip ended" for one product in one country for six hours. The state machine rejects 300,000 fare events.
One of the {{consumers}} consumer teams reads the change stream with a bug that skips versions; their receipts disagree with the trip state for 0.4% of trips and nobody notices for a week.

templates.title: Marketplace replay platform to evaluate dispatch policy changes offline
templates.subtopic: historical state capture, deterministic replay, counterfactual limits

sections.scenario: A marketplace's dispatch policy decides which driver is offered which request, whether to wait a few seconds to batch requests, and how far away a driver may be sent. Teams want to test changes (a new matching objective, a longer batching window, a new radius for airports) before running a live experiment. They ask for a replay platform: take what actually happened in {{cities}} cities over the last {{history_days}} days (requests, driver positions and states, trip outcomes) and replay it through a candidate policy to estimate wait times, match rates, cancellations, driver idle time and earnings. About {{policies}} candidate policies a week should be evaluated. Precise driver locations may be kept for at most {{location_retention}} under the data-retention policy.
sections.problem: Design the platform: what is captured from production and how, how a historical period is reconstructed into a starting state plus an event stream, how a candidate policy runs against it, how the simulated world reacts to decisions the real world never saw (a driver who was matched differently, a rider who waited longer), what metrics come out, and how results are compared and trusted. Say what replay cannot answer and how the platform tells users so.
sections.constraints: Two runs of the same policy on the same period must give identical results. Each policy evaluation must cover enough city-days to detect a 2% change in average wait time. A full run should finish overnight. The platform must not touch production systems. Location data older than {{location_retention}} cannot be used at full precision.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and timings are hypothetical. The dispatch policy can be packaged as a library that takes the marketplace state and the pending requests and returns offers. A live experimentation system already exists (for example switchback tests that alternate policies by city and time block).
sections.criteria: Capture of a complete, privacy-compliant marketplace log (state snapshots plus ordered events, versioned schemas); deterministic simulation with a single clock and seeded randomness; explicit split between replayed exogenous inputs and modelled behaviour, with models calibrated and their range of validity known; calibration of the production policy as a gate; metrics with confidence intervals and enough city-days; parallelism by city and period with reproducible manifests; clear statements of what replay cannot answer and how it hands off to live experiments; compliance with retention and deletion; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can we just re-run history with the new policy?
clarifications.a: Only partly. Once the new policy makes a different match, what drivers and riders do next was never observed. You decide how the simulator models it.

clarifications.q: Do drivers accept every offer?
clarifications.a: No. Acceptance and cancellation depend on pickup distance, fare and time of day. Historical rates by those factors exist.

clarifications.q: Who uses the results?
clarifications.a: Policy teams before a live test, and reviewers deciding whether a live test is worth the risk.

clarifications.q: Does it need to model surge?
clarifications.a: Prices respond to supply and demand; you decide whether to hold prices at their historical values or simulate them, and say what each choice hides.

hints: Separate exogenous inputs (requests, drivers coming online) that can be replayed as they happened from endogenous behaviour (acceptances, cancellations, repositioning) that must be modelled once decisions diverge.
Determinism needs a seeded random source per simulated actor and a single simulated clock, not wall time.
Calibrate before you compare: replaying the historical policy must reproduce historical metrics within a known error, or no candidate result means anything.
followups: How do you capture the marketplace state at a moment, and how do you get from a starting state to the exact sequence of events that follows?
The candidate policy matches a driver to a rider who historically took a different driver. What happens to the driver who historically picked that rider up?
Replay says the candidate cuts wait time by 6%; the live switchback test shows 1%. How do you find out which is wrong?
How do you parallelise {{policies}} policies across {{cities}} cities overnight while keeping every run reproducible?
The location retention limit means older periods have only coarse locations. How do you still evaluate seasonal effects such as a holiday from last year?

rules.ask: Your acceptance model was fitted on decisions the old policy made. Where will it be most wrong for the new policy?
Replaying the production policy gives wait times 4% below what actually happened. Do you correct the model, or report results relative to that baseline? Why?
A city's simulation is sequential in time. What is your unit of parallelism, and how do you stop the largest city from deciding how long the night takes?
A new library version changes floating-point rounding in the policy and a few matches differ. Is the run still reproducible? How would you detect that?
If live experiments exist, what is replay for? Which decisions should it make, and which should it never make on its own?

incidents: Two runs of the same policy on the same city-week differ in average wait time by 1.8%, almost the size of the effect the team is trying to measure.

The replay of the current production policy over the last {{history_days}} days reproduces historical match rates within 1% in most cities, but in three cities it is off by 9%. Those cities had an outage of the driver location stream during the period.
A policy evaluated as better in replay is tested live and raises driver cancellations by 5%, because it sends drivers on pickups longer than any they were offered in the historical data.

A deletion request and the {{location_retention}} retention limit remove precise locations for part of the period while a two-week evaluation is in progress; reruns of last month's results no longer match.

templates.title: Freight load board: search, ranking and live price quotes for carriers
templates.subtopic: near-real-time index, quotes with expiry, booking consistency

sections.scenario: A digital freight marketplace connects shippers who need truckloads moved with carriers (from owner-operators to fleets) who move them. Shippers post loads with an origin, a destination, a pickup window, an equipment type (dry van, refrigerated, flatbed), weight and requirements. Carriers search the board on a phone or a desktop, see loads ranked for them with an upfront price, and book in a few taps. At any time about {{loads}} loads are open; about {{carriers}} carriers are active in a month, with up to {{searches}} searches a second at the morning peak. Each price shown is a quote valid for {{quote_minutes}} minutes; prices move with lane supply and demand, and a booked load must disappear from every other carrier's results quickly.
sections.problem: Design the load board: load ingestion and updates from shippers, the search index (by origin and destination areas, dates, equipment, weight), ranking for a carrier (deadhead distance from where the truck is or will be empty, lane preferences, history, price), how quotes are produced, cached and expire, and how booking works so that a load is never booked by two carriers and the price a carrier booked at is the one honoured.
sections.constraints: Search p99 under 300 ms. A load booked or cancelled must leave search results within 5 seconds. A quote, once shown, must be honoured at booking until it expires. Two carriers tapping "book" on the same load within the same second must not both succeed. Carriers must be eligible for the load (equipment, insurance, authority to operate, any shipper restrictions).
sections.assumptions: All volumes and timings are hypothetical, and pricing rules are this exercise's. A pricing model exists as a service that returns a price for a (load, carrier) pair in about 50 ms; it can also price a lane in bulk.
sections.criteria: Clear split of index, candidate retrieval, ranking and pricing; an index updated from a change stream of load state with a bounded lag and a check of the authoritative load state before showing or booking; quotes as first-class records with inputs, expiry and an honour rule; booking as an idempotent conditional write on load state, with clear outcomes for the losing carrier; eligibility filters applied before ranking; saved searches inverted (match new loads against stored queries); ranking that handles carriers without location and corrects for position bias; capacity for the morning peak and bulk uploads; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the price the same for every carrier?
clarifications.a: Assume it can differ by carrier only through documented factors in this exercise (for example a reliability bonus). You decide where the per-carrier part is computed.

clarifications.q: Where is the carrier's truck?
clarifications.a: Some carriers share live location; others enter where they will be empty and when. Many do neither.

clarifications.q: Can shippers change a load after posting?
clarifications.a: Yes: pickup windows, weight and requirements change, and loads get cancelled. Each change may change the price.

clarifications.q: What happens when a quote expires during booking?
clarifications.a: You decide; say what the carrier sees.

clarifications.q: Do carriers save searches?
clarifications.a: Yes, and they want a notification when a matching load appears.

hints: Separate the index (which loads match) from the ranking and pricing (in what order, at what price). Pricing every match on every search is the expensive part.
A quote is a record with an id, the price, the inputs it depended on and an expiry; booking checks the quote, not a fresh price.
The booking decision is a conditional write on the load's state, not a search-index update.
followups: Walk through one search: what is queried, how many candidates come back, which are priced, and what is cached.
Two carriers book the same load 200 ms apart. Which records change, in what order, and what does the second carrier see?
A shipper edits the pickup window on a load that has 300 live quotes. What happens to those quotes?
How do you serve saved searches for {{carriers}} carriers without running every saved search on every new load?
How would you measure whether ranking is helping carriers, given that carriers mostly book what they see first?

rules.ask: Your index refreshes every second, but a booked load must disappear within 5 seconds under peak write load. Where else must you check that a load is still open?
A carrier in a rural area is 150 miles from the nearest load. How does your origin search behave when the nearby cells are empty?
You cache prices per lane. The pricing model is updated mid-morning. How long do carriers see the old prices, and is that a quote you must honour?
The booking write succeeds but the confirmation to the app times out. The carrier taps book again. What happens?
Your ranking model is trained on clicks and bookings from the old ranking. What bias does that create, and how do you correct for it?

incidents: Two carriers both receive a booking confirmation for the same refrigerated load; both trucks arrive at the shipper's dock the next morning.

A pricing model update goes out at 9:00 and raises quotes on several busy lanes by 30% for two hours before it is rolled back. About 1,100 loads were booked at those prices, and every quote issued in that time was valid for {{quote_minutes}} minutes.
A large shipper uploads 25,000 loads at 7:58, just before the morning peak. Index lag reaches four minutes, and carriers book loads that the shipper had already cancelled in the same upload.
Carriers who share live location see good loads near them; carriers who do not share location see mostly loads 300 miles away, and their bookings fall by half over a month.

templates.title: City-level marketplace health metrics for a thousand cities
templates.subtopic: definitions as code, backfills, per-city anomaly alerting

sections.scenario: A marketplace operates rides and delivery in {{cities}} cities, from megacities with millions of trips a week to small towns with a few hundred. City operations teams and leadership watch about {{metrics}} health metrics per city: completed trips, request-to-match rate, pickup time and its accuracy against the shown estimate, rider and driver cancellation rates, unfulfilled requests, surge exposure, driver utilisation, courier wait at restaurants, and others. Today each team computes its own version in its own notebooks, the numbers disagree, and alerts are hand-tuned for the largest cities only. You are asked to build one platform: metric definitions written once, refreshed for every city every {{freshness}}, kept for {{history_years}} years, and alerted on automatically.
sections.problem: Design the platform. Cover how a metric is defined (as code: source tables, filters, grain, numerator and denominator, time zone, owner, version), how definitions are reviewed and changed, how metrics are computed incrementally and backfilled when a definition changes or late data arrives, how restatements are recorded, and how anomaly detection works across cities of very different sizes so that teams trust the alerts.
sections.constraints: Every metric is computed per city in the city's local time (days and hours), including cities that change clocks for daylight saving time. A definition change must never silently rewrite history: old and new versions must be comparable. A backfill must not delay the regular updates every {{freshness}}. Alerts should reach the city's own team, and the platform should page no one for noise.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and timings are hypothetical. Trip, request, driver-status and order tables exist in a warehouse with event times in UTC; city boundaries and time zones are in a versioned reference table.
sections.criteria: Metrics as versioned code with owners, review and tests; ratios stored as numerator and denominator and rolled up correctly; a fine local-time grain with daylight-saving handling from a versioned time zone reference; incremental computation with a lateness window and explicit restatements recorded with reasons; backfills isolated in capacity and priority from regular runs; definition changes computed side by side and the detector re-baselined; city boundaries versioned with history mapped through merges and splits; anomaly detection scaled to volume (expected counts, seasonality, significance, minimum volume) with an alert budget and routing to owners; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Who owns a metric definition?
clarifications.a: Each metric needs one owning team. Today nobody owns most of them.

clarifications.q: Do cities ever change?
clarifications.a: Yes. Cities are merged, split, and have their boundaries redrawn; a metric's history must still make sense.

clarifications.q: What counts as an anomaly?
clarifications.a: A change the city team would act on. A 50% drop in completed trips in a town with ten trips an hour may be one quiet hour.

clarifications.q: Can late data change yesterday?
clarifications.a: Yes. Trips finish, fares are adjusted and cancellations are reversed for days afterwards.

clarifications.q: Which numbers does leadership see?
clarifications.a: A weekly review uses the same metrics; they want them stable once reviewed.

hints: A metric definition is code with a version and an owner; the platform compiles it into queries. A ratio metric stores its numerator and denominator separately so it can be rolled up correctly.
Compute on a grain fine enough to roll up (city × local hour × product) and derive days, weeks and regions from it.
Anomaly detection for a small city needs a different model from a large one: use expected counts with seasonality and a significance test, not a fixed percentage.
followups: Show me the definition of "rider cancellation rate" in your format, including what happens to a request re-matched to a second driver.
The owner changes that definition to exclude cancellations within two minutes of request. How is history handled, and what do dashboards show?
How do you schedule a {{history_years}}-year backfill for every city without delaying today's updates?
How do you alert on {{cities}} cities × {{metrics}} metrics without paging anyone for noise? What is your false-alert budget?
A daylight-saving change gives one city a 25-hour day. What do the hourly and daily metrics show, and what does the anomaly detector do?

rules.ask: Two teams want slightly different "match rate" definitions. Do you allow both? How does a dashboard reader know which one they are looking at?
Show me how one trip at 23:30 local time on the night clocks go back is assigned to an hour and a day.
In a town with 40 trips a day, how often does your threshold fire on ordinary days? How did you work that out?
A backfill changes last quarter's numbers that leadership already reviewed. What do they see, and how do they know why it changed?
You have a cancellation rate per city. How do you compute the region's rate from the cities, and what goes wrong if you average the city rates?

incidents: The new "rider cancellation rate" definition is deployed on a Monday morning; within an hour every one of the {{cities}} cities fires a cancellation alert, because the detector compares the new definition with history computed under the old one.
Two neighbouring cities are merged into one operating city. Their history disappears from dashboards, and the merged city's detector has no baseline.

A backfill of {{history_years}} years for a new metric starts on Friday evening and takes the warehouse capacity the regular jobs use; Saturday's regular updates, due every {{freshness}}, are four hours late during a holiday weekend.
Small cities fire about 300 alerts a week, almost all noise; city teams mute them, and a real drop in one town (a payments outage affecting a local card network) goes unseen for a day.

templates.title: Two business units, two trips tables: consolidating after a reorganisation
templates.subtopic: competing sources of truth, migration across teams

difference: one table counts a trip as completed when the driver ends it, the other only when the fare is finalised
one table records a batched delivery as one trip, the other as one trip per order
one table keeps cancelled trips that charged a fee, the other drops every cancelled trip

sections.scenario: After a reorganisation, the rides and delivery business units now report to one leader, and your team has been asked to own trip data for both. Each unit built its own trips table years ago. They overlap (some products, such as package deliveries made by ride drivers, were recorded by both units), and they disagree: {{difference}}. Weekly completed-trip counts differ by about {{gap}} between the two for the same cities. {{consumers}} dashboards, models and finance reports read one table or the other, and each unit's data team believes its table is the right one. Leadership wants one trips table within {{months}} months.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead the consolidation: how you find out who depends on what, how the definitions are decided and by whom, what the target looks like, how consumers migrate without breaking finance or pricing, what happens to the old tables, and how you keep both data teams engaged when one of them will feel it lost. Then tell me about a real time you consolidated competing sources of truth across teams, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not manage either unit's data team. Finance closes the quarter on one of the tables in seven weeks. Neither table can simply be switched off: some consumers have no owner.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence first (consumers from query logs and lineage, row-level reconciliation with every difference classified); a target that settles grain and carries both definitions explicitly where both are needed, with named owners and a decision record; a migration plan ordered by consumer criticality with parallel running, compatibility views with an end date, and a freeze around finance close; a plan for unowned consumers (identify, notify, brown-out, retire); both teams given real ownership in the result; measures of progress; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does leadership have a preferred table?
clarifications.a: No. They want one answer and have asked you to recommend it.

clarifications.q: Is either definition wrong?
clarifications.a: Both are defensible for their original purpose. They answer different questions.

clarifications.q: Do you know every consumer?
clarifications.a: Query logs show readers by account, but many are service accounts with no clear owner.

clarifications.q: Can the target keep both definitions?
clarifications.a: That is your call. Say what it costs.

hints: Separate the grain question (what one row is) from the definition questions (which rows count as completed). One table can carry both definitions as columns or flags.
Make the difference measurable: reconcile the two tables row by row for a few cities and classify every difference.
Plan the migration around the consumers that matter most (finance, pricing, payments) and the ones nobody owns.
followups: Your reconciliation shows that {{gap}} difference is mostly one cause, but 0.3% is unexplained. Do you start the migration?
One unit's data lead says the new table is "their table with extra steps" and their team stops attending. What do you do?
Finance wants nothing to change before the quarter closes. How does your plan respect that without slipping {{months}} months?
A third of the consumers have no owner. How do you migrate or retire them safely?
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: On the day you switch, one unowned pricing job reads the old table and fails silently. How would you have found it beforehand?
How long does the compatibility view live, and what stops it from becoming a third trips table?
Who has the final say on what "completed" means, and how is that decision recorded so it is not reopened every quarter?
What exactly would you ask leadership to decide, and what would you decide yourself?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Growing a data platform team from 3 to 12 in two quarters without lowering the bar
templates.subtopic: hiring quality, onboarding, keeping the system running while growing

platform: the streaming platform that carries trip and location events
the batch platform that computes driver and courier earnings inputs
the feature platform that serves pricing and ETA models
complication: half of the new roles are in an office eight time zones away
the most senior of the three engineers plans to move teams at the end of the first quarter
the recruiting team can schedule only two interview loops a week for your roles

sections.scenario: You lead a team of three engineers who own {{platform}}. The platform's load has tripled in a year, on-call receives about {{pages}} pages a week, and the three engineers spend most of their time keeping it running. You have approval to grow to twelve engineers within two quarters. There is a complication: {{complication}}. Your manager says the platform cannot have a serious outage during the growth.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would do it: what roles you hire for and in what order, how you design a selection process that tests what the job actually needs and is consistent between interviewers, how you protect the three current engineers' time, how new people get productive and safe on call, and how you know at the end of two quarters that the bar held. Then tell me about a real time you grew a team or brought several people on at once, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The three current engineers must also interview and onboard. You cannot pause on-call. Any process you design is your own team's; you are not changing any company-wide hiring policy.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Hiring plan derived from what the platform needs (skills, seniority mix, order of roles, including the complication); a selection process with written criteria, work-sample exercises, trained and calibrated interviewers and a decision rule that resists pressure; operational load reduced early so current engineers can hire and onboard; onboarding treated as a product (runbooks, shadowing, graded on-call); measures that show whether quality held (new-hire ramp time, on-call incidents, peer feedback, attrition); protects the existing team; real example with what went wrong and what changed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Can you hire contractors or borrow engineers?
clarifications.a: You can borrow one engineer from a neighbouring team for one quarter.

clarifications.q: Do the twelve all have to be senior?
clarifications.a: No. The mix is yours, within the approved budget.

clarifications.q: What is "the bar"?
clarifications.a: You define it: what someone must be able to do on this team, and how you will check.

clarifications.q: How long does onboarding take today?
clarifications.a: Nobody has onboarded anyone for two years. There is no written runbook for most alerts.

hints: Write down what the team must be able to do in six months; derive the roles and their order from it, not from a headcount number.
A consistent bar needs written criteria per role, structured exercises close to the work, and interviewers who calibrate against each other.
Hiring fast with a team that is drowning in pages fails. Reduce operational load early and make onboarding a product.
followups: In the first month you have four strong candidates for the same role and one interviewer slot a day. What do you do?
Interviewers disagree sharply on a candidate. How do you decide, and what does that disagreement tell you about your process?
How does a new engineer go from day one to taking on-call alone, and how do you know they are ready?
Two quarters in, you have hired ten, not nine. How do you check that the people hired late were held to the same standard as the first?
In your real example, what went wrong with a hire or with onboarding, and what did you change?

rules.ask: Referrals fill your pipeline quickly. What does that do to the range of backgrounds on the team, and does it matter for this platform?
Show me two criteria from your rubric for this role, and what a weak and a strong answer look like for each.
If you hire mostly senior engineers, who does the work that seniors do not want, and how long do they stay?
Who writes those runbooks while the three engineers are on call and interviewing? What do you stop doing to make room?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Product wants real-time earnings in 4 weeks; the honest estimate is 12
templates.subtopic: correctness of money shown to people, delivery under pressure

audience: drivers and couriers in the app
drivers and couriers in the app and in a weekly email
reason: a launch event already announced for one region
a competitor's similar feature that product has seen in the press
complaints that earnings appear a day late

sections.scenario: Product wants a real-time earnings view for {{audience}}: trips and deliveries completed today, fares, tips, incentives earned so far, and the running total for the week. Today earnings appear the next day from a nightly batch that pulls from {{sources}} sources (trips, fare adjustments, tips that arrive hours later, incentive programmes, cancellation fees, support adjustments and more). The product manager has promised it in four weeks because of {{reason}}. Your honest estimate, with the correctness the numbers need, is twelve weeks. You are the technical lead.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would handle it: how you make your estimate credible, what you would propose that could ship in four weeks without showing anyone a wrong number about their own pay, how you negotiate with the product manager and their leadership, and what you do if they insist on the full scope in four weeks. Then tell me about a real time your estimate disagreed sharply with a committed date, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Numbers about a person's pay must reconcile with their pay statement; a real-time number that is later reduced erodes trust far more than a late one. You cannot add people within the four weeks. The nightly batch remains the source for payouts.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: An estimate broken into parts with explicit risks and what would change it; a first slice that is correct by construction and labelled honestly, with a path to the full scope; negotiation that respects the product manager's goals and goes to the decider together, with date, scope and correctness trade-offs visible; refusal to show people wrong numbers about their pay, with reasons; a reconciliation plan with payouts; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: What makes the estimate twelve weeks?
clarifications.a: That is what you must explain. Assume the hardest parts are tips and adjustments that arrive late, incentive rules computed only in the batch, and reconciliation with payouts.

clarifications.q: Is the four-week date public?
clarifications.a: It has been mentioned to the region's partners, not announced publicly.

clarifications.q: Does product know the estimate?
clarifications.a: They heard "about three months" in a hallway and treated it as padding.

clarifications.q: Who has the authority to change the date?
clarifications.a: The product manager's director.

hints: Break the estimate into parts with their own uncertainty; show what is known work and what is risk.
Look for a first slice that is exact by construction (for example, completed trips and their base fare, labelled "so far today, before tips and adjustments") and a path to the rest.
Make the trade-off visible to the person who decides: date, scope and correctness. Never quietly trade correctness away.
followups: Walk me through the twelve weeks: what are the parts, which are risky, and what would make it eight?
What exactly would ship in four weeks, what would it be labelled, and how do you know it will not show a number that later goes down?
The director says ship the full scope in four weeks and fix it later. What do you say?
Week three, the first slice works but the tips feed is two hours late on weekends. Do you launch?
In your real example, what did you personally do when the estimate and the date disagreed, and how did it turn out?

rules.ask: How many weeks does overtime actually buy you on this work, and what does it cost in month three?
Show me the first slice's exact contents and the sentence on screen that tells a driver what is and is not included.
Your last two estimates on this team were 40% low. Why should product trust this one?
What do you put in front of the director, and how do you make sure the product manager is not surprised by it?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: A service-account key with warehouse access published in a public repository
templates.subtopic: credential exposure, scoping access, blameless follow-through

scope: read access to the trip and location tables
read and write access to the analytics schemas, including rider contact tables
read access to every table the data platform's scheduler can reach
found_by: an external researcher through the disclosure programme
an engineer on another team who saw it while browsing

sections.scenario: A long-lived key for a service account that your team owns was committed to a public code repository by an engineer on your team, inside a configuration file for a side project. It has been public for {{hours}} hours. The account has {{scope}}. It was reported by {{found_by}}. It is 18:40 on a Friday. You are the most senior engineer on the team; the security team has an on-call engineer, and privacy and legal have on-call contacts.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead your part of the response in the first hour, the first day and the following weeks. Cover containment, establishing whether the key was used and what was read, working with security, privacy and legal, what happens to the jobs that use that account, how you treat the engineer who committed it, and what you change so a key like this cannot leak or cannot matter if it does. Then tell me about a real security or data-exposure incident you were involved in, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not decide whether people or regulators are notified; privacy and legal do, using your facts. Fourteen scheduled jobs, including the nightly earnings inputs, run as that service account. Access logs on the warehouse are kept for 30 days.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Immediate containment (revoke the key, accept and manage the job failures, issue a scoped replacement through a secret manager) with security involved from the first minutes; evidence-based scoping from access logs (which tables, rows, times, source addresses), preserved for investigation, distinguishing the jobs' normal use from anything else; clear, factual handoff to privacy and legal, who decide on notification; a blameless approach to the engineer that still fixes the conditions; prevention that removes long-lived keys (short-lived credentials, workload identity, least privilege, secret scanning in commits) and limits blast radius; a plan for the other keys; real example with personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anyone used the key?
clarifications.a: Unknown when you are paged.

clarifications.q: Can the key simply be revoked?
clarifications.a: Yes, but the fourteen jobs fail until they have a new credential.

clarifications.q: Has the commit been removed?
clarifications.a: The engineer deleted the file in a new commit ten minutes ago; the key is still in the repository's history and may have been copied.

clarifications.q: Is the engineer still online?
clarifications.a: Yes, and visibly upset.

hints: Revoke first. A published key is compromised whether or not anyone used it; deleting the commit does not undo the leak.
The question privacy and legal need answered is "what was accessed, by whom, from where", from logs, not from guesses.
Ask why a single long-lived key could read so much, and why it could be copied into a file at all.
followups: Revoking the key will make the nightly earnings inputs fail tonight. Do you revoke now or after the run? Who decides?
The warehouse logs show three queries from an unfamiliar address two hours after the commit. What do you do with that?
What do you say to the engineer who committed the key, tonight and next week?
The review finds 40 other long-lived keys across the data platform. How do you get rid of them without breaking everything?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and what changed afterwards?

rules.ask: Fourteen jobs use that account. Walk me through how they get a new credential tonight without anyone pasting it somewhere new.
The logs show queries by the service account from its usual job hosts and from one unknown address. How do you tell the jobs' queries apart from an attacker's using the same key?
What does the rest of the team learn about reporting their own mistakes from how you handle this?
Scanning catches known key formats. What about a credential that does not look like one, and what makes a leak harmless even when scanning misses it?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a real-time, city-by-city marketplace
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, real-time and per-city operation

angle: the data model and how it handled change
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the biggest latency or cost decision
city_feature: rules that differ by city and change every week
every city's day and week in its own time zone
a city that keeps working when its region is cut off

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change to serve a real-time marketplace operating city by city, where its outputs must be at most {{freshness}} old and where it must handle {{city_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if its outputs had to be at most {{freshness}} old and it had to handle {{city_feature}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The marketplace setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with the alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible freshness analysis that names the first part that cannot keep up and an incremental change for it; a concrete path to the city feature; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a streaming system?
clarifications.a: No. A batch system is fine; the second half asks what would change.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to schemas, keys, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the real-time question, name the first part of your system that cannot meet {{freshness}} and why.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which part of your system cannot produce outputs within {{freshness}}, and what would you change first?
How would you add {{city_feature}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Which outputs of that batch would actually be worth having within {{freshness}}, and which would not? How do you decide?
One city is a hundred times larger than the median. Where does that show up in your design: partitioning, compute or the people who operate it?
